Camera Raw Decoding
Camera raw media formats are so named because they capture raw color space data directly from the 
sensor of whatever digital cinema camera did the recording. Raw image data is not human readable, 
and must be debayered or demosaiced to convert the original raw data into image data that can be 
handed off to DaVinci Resolve’s image processing pipeline.
There are four ways you can control how camera raw media is debayered into a useful, “normalized” 
image for adjustment or output:
	 The Camera Raw panel of the Project Settings contain groups of parameters that correspond to 
every camera raw media format that’s supported by DaVinci Resolve. Using these parameters 
in the Camera Raw panel, you can override the original camera metadata that was written at 
the time of recording, and make simultaneous adjustments to all camera raw media throughout 
your project.
	 The Image Panel in the Inspector also contains the controls for every raw media format 
that’s supported by DaVinci Resolve. Allowing you to select all, some, or individual clips 
for raw debayering.
	 The Camera Raw palette in the Color page lets you individually adjust Camera Raw parameters 
for individual clips in the Timeline.
	 When you use Resolve Color Management (RCM) in a project that uses Camera Raw formats, 
color science data from each camera manufacturer is used to debayer or demosaic each camera 
raw file to specific color primaries with linear gamma, so that all image data from the source is 
preserved and made available to DaVinci Resolve’s color managed image processing pipeline. 
As a result, the Camera Raw project settings and Camera Raw palette of the Color page are 
disabled, because RCM is controlling the debayering of all camera raw clips, and all image data 
from the raw file is available for conversion to the Timeline Color Space you choose to work with 
as you grade.
For more information about each of the Camera Raw formats that can be adjusted in 
DaVinci Resolve, jump to this chapter: Camera Raw Settings.

Chapter 22
Importing 
and Conforming 
Timelines
Generally speaking, “conforming” a project describes the process of importing a 
project exchange file from another post-production application, and automatically 
relinking each clip in the imported timeline to the high-quality media files 
each clip corresponds to.
If you need to continue editing, color correct, or finish a project that was put together in another 
application, you can import via the EDL, AAF, or XML project exchange formats. When you go through 
the process of conforming a project, you use the imported project data to arrange the clips in the 
Media Pool into a timeline that constitutes the program that’s about to be graded.
This chapter walks you through the process of preparing timelines in other applications prior to moving 
them into DaVinci Resolve and covers which effects have counterparts in the DaVinci Resolve timeline. 
It ends with instructions on how to set up to compare a reference movie to the Timeline.

Preparing to Move Your Project 
to DaVinci Resolve
When you’re preparing to move a project from another NLE to DaVinci Resolve, there are a few steps 
you can take to make your work more organized.
Move Clips to the Lowest Video Track
Editors often use the multiple tracks NLEs offer for simple clip organization in the edit of a scene. While 
this is convenient for offline editorial, it is less convenient when you’re trying to conform, grade, finish, 
and render the media used by a project as quickly and efficiently as possible.
For this reason, it’s a good idea to move all clips that are not stacked or superimposed as part of a 
compositing operation down to track V1 of the Timeline in your NLE. This produces a simplified edit 
that has many advantages. The project becomes smaller to move because there’s less media in the 
Timeline, and consequently becomes faster to render. Furthermore, the colorist is spared confusion 
because this eliminates “hidden” media that is nonetheless connected to other clips that can be seen.
It’s also helpful, once you’ve reorganized the Timeline, to eliminate any empty tracks that are left. 
This can be done from within DaVinci Resolve, but doing it in your NLE further simplifies the project 
import process.
Organize Unsupported Media Files
Depending on your workflow and on the NLE you’re working with, there may be clips using formats 
that are unsupported in DaVinci Resolve. Unsupported generators, media formats, and other effects 
constructs may simply not be seen in DaVinci Resolve, and will consequently appear as unlinked clips.
If you know this in advance, you can move all such clips into dedicated tracks where they can be 
isolated, and the track can be turned off to hide the unsupported clips, simplifying timeline navigation. 
This also saves the colorist from the need to worry about why there are offline clips in the Timeline at 
3 o’clock in the morning, immediately before starting a render.
Creating an Offline Reference Movie
Even though the colorist in any given workflow is likely to be building new grades from scratch, 
it can be valuable to have a reference movie showing any color corrections, filters, or effects that 
the offline editor applied during the editing process. This offline reference can be imported into a 
DaVinci Resolve project, and used as a split-screen reference whenever there’s some question about 
a look or effect from the offline edit.
Offline reference movies also serve as a useful tool when conforming a project in the Edit page. 
After project conform, you can compare the project as seen in the Record Viewer with the 
synchronized offline movie as seen in the Source Viewer set to Offline mode. This makes it easy to 
scrub through a project to make sure that each clip has imported correctly and is in sync. 
More information about using offline reference movies appears later in this chapter.

Mixed Frame Sizes and Mixed Codecs
Most NLEs can freely mix media using different frame sizes, different codecs, and different frame rates. 
DaVinci Resolve deals with these combinations in different ways, depending on what settings you’ve 
selected in the Project Settings.
	 Mixing Frame Sizes: Mixed frame sizes are easily handled. The Set Timeline Resolution To 
parameter in the Project Settings panel of the Project Settings dictates the current resolution of 
the project. Any clips with a frame size that doesn’t match the project is resized according to the 
option selected in the Image Scaling panel of the Project Settings. You can, of course, always 
manually readjust the sizing of any clip if you want to make a specific adjustment. All resizing is 
done using the optical-quality resizing algorithms in DaVinci Resolve. 
For more information, jump to this chapter: Sizing and Image Stabilization.
	 Mixing Codecs: Mixed codecs are also not a problem, as long as the different codecs used by 
the media in the project you’re importing are compatible with the list of codecs and formats that 
DaVinci Resolve supports. For more information about the currently supported list of codecs and 
formats, check the Blackmagic Design support page for DaVinci Resolve. This list is updated often 
with newly supported formats.
Mixed Frame Rates
DaVinci Resolve also supports mixed frame rates, although there is a setting you must choose to 
ensure the best results for the NLE you’re importing from. By default, mixed clip frame rate support 
is enabled via the “Mixed frame rate format” pop-up menu that appears either in the Master Project 
Settings, or in the Import AAF or XML dialog. 
The different options available in the “Mixed frame rate format” pop-up are available to let you conform 
projects using the method of mixed frame rate calculation used by the NLE a project was originally 
edited in; different NLEs have different ways of mixing frame rates, and that used by Final Cut Pro 7 is 
different from that used by Final Cut Pro X or Avid Media Composer. If you need to change this setting, 
you must do so before you import any media into the Media Pool; once the Media Pool is populated, 
this setting can no longer be changed.
Mixed frame rate format selection
467
Ingest and Organize Media | Chapter 22 Importing and Conforming Timelines
MEDIA

===== Page 468 =====
This Mixed frame rate format pop-up menu is also found in the Load AAF and Load XML dialogs. 
DaVinci Resolve automatically chooses a setting from the “Mixed frame rate format” pop-up menu 
that corresponds to the project file you’re importing, but in some cases you can override this 
setting if necessary. For projects sent from Final Cut Pro, you can choose either “Final Cut Pro 7” or 
“Final Cut Pro X” to match the type of project you’re importing. On the other hand, you should choose 
“Resolve” for projects imported from Premiere Pro, Smoke, Media Composer, or other NLEs.
When “Mixed frame rate format” is set to anything but None, DaVinci Resolve conforms and processes 
all clips in the Timeline to play at the project’s frame rate. For example, 23.98, 29.97, 30, 50, 59.94, 
and 60 fps clips will all play at 24 fps if that’s what “Timeline frame rate” is set to in the Master Project 
Settings. Clips with different source frame rates will be retimed to match the Timeline conform 
frame rate. 
The Retime process that’s used to render clips with differing frame rates can be changed for 
individual clips via the Retime Process parameter in the Edit page Inspector, or it can be changed 
project-wide using the Retime Process parameter found in the Frame Interpolation panel of the 
Master Project Settings. 
For more information on how each of the three available options work, jump to this chapter: 
System and User Preferences. 
If you choose “None,” then clips with frame rates that aren’t equal to the Timeline frame rate will ignore 
their original frame rate and will play at the Timeline rate, resulting in either faster or slower motion, 
depending on the difference between the original and Timeline frame rates.
NOTE: Because DPX files often either lack or have incorrect frame rate information in 
the header data, you may need to select None when conforming a project using image 
sequences to make sure your media is not incorrectly interpreted.
How clips in mixed frame rate timelines are rendered depends on whether the Render Settings are set 
to render individual source clips or one single clip. When you render the Timeline as ”Individual Source 
Clips,” then all clips are rendered individually at their original frame rate. If you select ”Single Clip,” 
then all clips are converted to the “Timeline frame rate” frame rate setting, and rendered as a single 
media file.

About Supported Color Corrections
At the time of this writing, only Final Cut Pro X XML projects are capable of exporting color correction 
data that can be imported as primary grades in DaVinci Resolve. For obvious reasons, color correction 
import is a one-way street, and imported color corrections cannot be output back to Final Cut Pro. 
Imported Final Cut Pro X color adjustments appear in the Color page as primary corrections.
Other workflows for importing color correction information from other applications are available using 
ColorTrace to import grade data from CDLs (Color Decision Lists). 
For more information, jump to this chapter: Copying and Importing Grades Using ColorTrace.
About Supported Transitions
EDLs are the most restrictive when it comes to transition support in DaVinci Resolve, as only Cross 
Dissolves will be read. Any other transitions appearing in an EDL will be automatically converted to a 
Cross Dissolve of the same duration when it’s imported into DaVinci Resolve.

About Supported Opacity, Position, Scale, and Rotation Settings
When importing XML project files from Final Cut Pro X, Premiere Pro, or legacy Final Cut Pro 7, DaVinci 
Resolve supports the import of Opacity, Position, Scale, and Rotation settings. Imported Composite 
and Transform settings for any given clip appear in the Inspector of the Edit page, or in the Edit Sizing 
mode of the Sizing palette in the Color page. If these settings have been keyframed, the animation will 
appear in DaVinci Resolve.
When importing AAF files from Media Composer or Symphony, DaVinci Resolve supports the 
import of Opacity, Resize, and 3D Warp effects, which are converted into Pan, Tilt, Zoom, and Rotate 
settings in DaVinci Resolve, located in the Edit page Inspector or the Edit Sizing mode of the Sizing 
palette in the Color page. 
About Flip and Flop Support
When importing AAF project files from Media Composer or Symphony, Flip, Flop, and Flip-Flop effects 
are converted into the equivalent horizontal and vertical Flip toggles in DaVinci Resolve, located in the 
Edit page Inspector or the Edit Sizing mode of the Sizing palette in the Color page.
Pitch and Yaw
When importing AAF files from Media Composer or Symphony, DaVinci Resolve supports the 
import of Pitch and Yaw 3D Warp effects, which are converted into equivalent Pitch and Yaw settings 
in DaVinci Resolve, located in the Edit page Inspector or the Edit Sizing mode of the Sizing palette 
in the Color page.
About “Ken Burns Effect” and Dynamic Zoom
If you import a project from Final Cut Pro X with clips that use the Ken Burns effect for creating pan and 
scan animation, then the Dynamic Zoom parameters (found in the Edit page Inspector when a clip is 
selected) for each affected clip will be populated with an equivalent animated effect.
About Speed Effects
DaVinci Resolve supports the import of speed effects from different applications, but different project 
formats have different speed effect support.
	 EDL: DaVinci Resolve only supports the import of linear speed effects when importing EDLs. 
	 XML: DaVinci Resolve supports the import of both linear and variable speed effects when 
importing XML project files from Premiere Pro, Final Cut Pro 7, and Final Cut Pro X. As of DaVinci 
Resolve version 11.1, XML from Final Cut Pro X can also provide information about whether frame 
blending or optical flow is used, as well as information about the Bezier curve transitions of 
speed effects.
	 AAF: DaVinci Resolve supports the import of both linear and variable speed effects when 
importing AAF files from Media Composer or Symphony that use Timewarp effects.
DaVinci Resolve has high-fidelity conversion of variable-speed speed effect data from other 
applications, accomplished by creating one speed keyframe per frame for each affected clip. 
However, you may see small variations between the resulting speed effect in DaVinci Resolve and an 
offline reference movie exported from the original NLE if you haven’t set the Retime Process setting to 
the same type of speed interpolation that the original NLE was using. 
471

In other words, if you created a Timewarp speed effect in Media Composer that uses FluidMotion to 
create smooth slow motion effects, then you’ll want to make sure to change either the project-wide 
or clip-specific Retime Process setting to Optical Flow so that the speed effects in DaVinci Resolve 
best match those in Media Composer. 
For more information on speed effects in DaVinci Resolve, jump to this chapter: Speed Effects.
About Nested Sequences and Compound Clips
DaVinci Resolve supports the import of compound clips from Final Cut Pro X and of nested sequences 
from legacy Final Cut Pro 7. Both appear within DaVinci Resolve as compound clips, in both the 
Timeline and the Media Pool. Compound clips with mixed frame rates are supported, as well as multi-
cam and A/V synchronized clips from Final Cut Pro X, which are represented in DaVinci Resolve as 
compound clips. 
For more information on creating and using compound clips in DaVinci Resolve, jump to this 
chapter: Take Selectors, Compound Clips, and Nested Timelines.

About Supported Still Image Formats
DaVinci Resolve supports the import of greater-than-one-frame-in-duration TIF, JPG, PNG, DPX, 
TGA, and DNG still image files that appear in Final Cut Pro X, Final Cut Pro 7, and Premiere Pro 
XML files, and AAF files exported from Media Composer. These clips appear as ordinary clips in 
the DaVinci Resolve Timeline. Export of still images is limited to Final Cut Pro 7 and Final Cut Pro X 
XML formats.
About Supported Alpha Channels
Media with embedded alpha channels is supported for any project as long as it’s in a media format that 
DaVinci Resolve supports; this includes TIFF, OpenEXR image sequence formats, and four-channel 
QuickTime formats such as ProRes 4444, DNxHR 444, and QuickTime Animation. Alpha channels are 
automatically enabled, and can be used for compositing directly within the DaVinci Resolve Timeline.
Alpha channels can be exported in round-trip workflows when rendering individual source clips. 
However, when rendering a program as a single clip, all composited effects are rendered together to 
produce a single output media file. 
For more information on rendering clips with alpha channels, jump to this chapter:  
Delivery Effects Processing.
About Imported Text Effects
DaVinci Resolve supports the import of text generators when importing XML project files from both 
Final Cut Pro X and Final Cut Pro 7. All imported text effects appear in the DaVinci Resolve Timeline as 
Basic text generators. Some, but not all, formatting parameters are imported, depending on the project 
file format being imported.
About Imported Audio in AAF Projects
Any combination of audio track types, channel map order, MXF and QuickTime files, and rendered or 
unrendered clips should import without problems.
NOTE: When exporting an AAF project, DaVinci Resolve is capable of writing mono media in 
stereo tracks.
Preparing Unsupported Clips and Effects You Want to Grade
If there is an unsupported effect within your NLE of choice that you want to move into DaVinci Resolve 
for grading (for example, clips with effects filters that are native to a particular NLE), here’s a simple 
workflow to follow.
To “bake” an effect into a clip you’re sending to DaVinci Resolve:
1	
Export that clip as a self-contained media file using whatever DaVinci Resolve-compatible 
mastering codec you prefer.
2	
Reimport the resulting media file into your project.
3	
Edit it into your project’s timeline to replace the original effects clip.
4	
Export a version of the resulting sequence for use in DaVinci Resolve.
473
Ingest and Organize Media | Chapter 22 Importing and Conforming Timelines
MEDIA

===== Page 474 =====
This is a good way of prepping the titles and effects of projects that you want to finish in DaVinci 
Resolve. If you create self-contained media files for all title clips and effects, then these elements 
will import cleanly and easily, and you can export a complete, texted version of your program out of 
DaVinci Resolve.
Additionally, if a composited clip is using unsupported effects (for example, a filtered still image with 
animated position that’s superimposed using the Overlay composite mode and set to 70% opacity), 
an ideal way to prep this clip for XML export to DaVinci Resolve is to set the composite mode to 
Normal, set Opacity to 100%, and then export the resulting clip as a self-contained QuickTime movie. 
Reimport the result, edit it back into the Timeline to replace the original superimposed clip, and then 
set its composite mode to Overlay and its Opacity to 70% to match the original settings. Now the 
unsupported effects are “baked” into the clip, but the effects that DaVinci Resolve does support are 
still live, and can be readjusted in context while grading.
Verifying Imported Timelines 
Using Offline References
DaVinci Resolve has a specific interface for comparing two versions of a program. This eliminates the 
need to edit a rendered version of a timeline as a superimposed clip within your timeline and provides 
many other features to aid this comparison without cluttering your timeline. 
By setting the Source Viewer in the Edit page to Offline mode, you can compare an Offline Reference 
Clip or Timeline to a currently open timeline, with both playheads ganged together, either side by 
side, or as a split screen, a box wipe, or difference operation, all of which will be visible via your video 
output device. As you play the Timeline, the Offline Reference Clip or timeline plays as well, making it 
easy to spot differences between the two. 
IMPORTANT: You need to make sure that the media you’ve imported or are using as an 
Offline Reference Clip has a valid timecode track with a start time that matches the timecode 
of the Timeline you’re comparing to, otherwise there will be an offset between the Timeline 
and offline reference that will make a comparison difficult to impossible. Small offsets can be 
corrected via an offset field in the Source Viewer while in offline mode, but large offsets will 
be impractical to correct.
Why Set Up An Offline Comparison?
However you set up an offline reference, this is a convenient way of comparing two versions of a 
program. There are several reasons for comparing an Offline Reference Clip to a timeline:
	 Verifying the clip order: If you’re unsure whether or not you’ve properly resolved reel conflicts or 
other problems that occurred while you were conforming a timeline, you can compare each edit 
to the offline version of the program to spot problems and identify the proper media that should 
correspond to any clip.
	 Recreating effects: If there are offline effects, such as temporary grades made in the NLE, or pan 
and scan transforms that you want to check, the Offline reference mode lets you split-screen your 
current grade against the Offline Reference Clip in the Color page.
	 Comparing two versions of a timeline: You can make a visual comparison a timeline with another 
version of that timeline to spot differences for evaluation.
	 Filling holes in timelines with missing or unlinked clips: Two options found in the Preferences > 
User > Editing > General settings, “Show offline clips through conform gaps,” and “Show offline 
474
Ingest and Organize Media | Chapter 22 Importing and Conforming Timelines
MEDIA

===== Page 475 =====
clips through missing clips,” let you set DaVinci Resolve to display Offline Reference Clip media to 
fill gaps in the Timeline or replace the contents of unlinked clips. This is typically done to resolve 
emergency situations when you need to proceed with a screening or review session despite the 
fact that you’re missing media for whatever reason. 
For more information, jump to this chapter: System and User Preferences.
NOTE: Typically, the flattened version of the program you’re given uses a low-quality codec, 
and contains effects and color correction that’s not final, which is why it’s called an Offline 
Reference Clip.
Assigning a Clip or Timeline for Offline Comparison
There are two ways you can assign an Offline Reference Clip or Timeline to a particular timeline for 
comparison. The easiest and most flexible way is to open a timeline, and then drag and drop a clip or 
timeline with matching timecode that you want to compare to from the Media Pool onto the Source 
Viewer in Offline mode.
To assign any clip or timeline to a specific timeline for comparison:
1	
Open the timeline you want to make the assignment to in the Edit page.
2	
Set the Source Viewer to Offline mode.
3	
Drag a clip or timeline with matching timecode that you want to assign onto the Source Viewer. 
The clip or timeline you dragged is immediately assigned to the open timeline as an Offline 
Reference Clip, and synced via timecode.
4	
In the Media Pool, right-click the Timeline you want to review against the Offline Reference 
Clip, and choose the reference clip or timeline you assigned from the Timelines > Link Offline 
Reference Clip submenu of that timeline’s contextual menu.
You can also add a clip to the Media Pool specifically as an Offline Reference Clip, making it easy 
to associate such a clip with a particular timeline by right-clicking that timeline in the Media Pool 
and choosing it from the Link Offline Video submenu. The idea is that if you or your client exports 
a flattened version of their edited sequence at the same time as they export the EDL, AAF, or XML 
project file they want graded, then you can compare the project data that’s imported into DaVinci 
Resolve to the actual video of the offline edit.
To assign an imported Offline Reference Clip to a specific timeline for comparison:
1	
Open the Media page, and use the Media Storage browser to find the flattened Offline Reference 
Clip that you want to use for comparison.
2	
Right-click the Offline Reference Clip file and choose Add as Offline Reference Clip.
3	
That clip appears with a small checkerboard badge in its icon in the Media Pool.

Conforming and Relinking Media
DaVinci Resolve has tools for managing the relationship between clips in the Media Pool, clips in 
timelines, and the links between each clip and its corresponding media file on disk. These tools 
support a variety of project workflows, and can help to resolve issues that may arise when importing 
projects of different formats and sources.
This section covers the available methods for conforming clips and relinking media. More information 
on the clip metadata that’s used to match clips with their source media is covered later in this chapter.
Conforming and Relinking During Project Import
When you import an AAF or XML file, DaVinci Resolve automatically relinks the imported clips in the 
Media Pool to their corresponding source media files on disk. At the same time, the imported timeline 
is conformed to those clips in the Media Pool. The result is a populated media pool, and a timeline 
containing the arranged clips. 
Because these steps typically happen together, it’s easy to overlook the distinction between a 
timeline’s relationship to clips in the Media Pool, and each clip’s relationship to its source media 
file on disk.
The workflow for importing an EDL makes this distinction more explicit. You’ll start by importing the 
required clips into the Media Pool, ensuring they have the correct reel names and timecode. This 
establishes the link between the Media Pool clips and the source media on disk. You’ll then import the 
EDL, which creates a timeline that attempts to conform itself to the media pool clips using reel name 
and timecode information.
Conforming and Relinking Existing Timelines and Clips
Sometimes, you may need to reconform or relink media after editing or grading has begun. 
For example, you might start a project using placeholder VFX or stock footage clips, then replace 
these with final versions of the same shots. Or, you may choose to edit using transcoded versions of 
camera raw media files, and later switch to the original camera media for grading and finishing. 
To support these workflows, DaVinci Resolve has a wide variety of tools for reconforming timelines 
and relinking media throughout the life of a project.
The Difference Between Conforming and Relinking
While the terms are often used interchangeably, conforming generally refers to matching clips 
in a timeline to the appropriate source clips in the Media Pool, and relinking refers to matching 
source clips in the Media Pool to their corresponding media files on disk. This recent change 
reflects the expanded relinking and conforming workflows available in DaVinci Resolve, so the 
author offers his apologies if these terms are used more loosely elsewhere in this manual.

===== Page 479 =====
The Difference Between 
Unlinked and Missing Clips
When it comes to the relationship between clips in the Media Pool and clips in a timeline, there’s an 
important distinction between clips that are unlinked, and clips that are missing. While both of these 
“offline” clip states look different in the timeline, their differences aren’t just cosmetic.
A missing clip in the Timeline (left) compared to an unlinked clip in the Timeline (right).
An unlinked clip is one that exists in the Media Pool, but has lost its connection to the 
corresponding media file on disk. However, because the unlinked clip and its metadata remain 
in your project’s timelines, it can be easily relinked to matching media with the Relink command 
(described later), or reconformed to previously imported or newly imported clips in specific bins of 
the Media Pool with the Reconform From Bins command (also described later).
A missing clip doesn’t exist in the Media Pool, but might still appear in the timelines of your project. 
If there isn’t a corresponding source clip in the Media Pool, its metadata is unavailable in the 
Metadata Editor, and any remote grades associated with that source clip are also lost. 
For more information about remote grades, jump to this chapter: Grade Management.
You can fix missing clips in a timeline in one of two ways:
	 If the “Automatically conform missing clips added to Media Pool” setting is enabled in the Project 
Settings > General Options panel, simply reimport the corresponding source clips into the Media 
Pool. Any missing clips with matching timecode and file names in the timeline will be reconformed. 
Note that this only occurs at the time of import, and doesn’t apply to matching clips that are 
already in the Media Pool. This setting must be disabled if you use collaborative workflows.
	 If the “Automatically conform missing clips added to Media Pool” setting is disabled in the Project 
Settings > General Options panel, reimport the missing media. Then either manually reconform 
them individually to the missing timeline clips with the Conform Lock with Media Pool Clip 
command, or use the Reconform From Bin(s) or Import Additional Clips With Loose/Tight Filename 
Match commands to simultaneously reconform multiple clips.
When you reconform the missing clips, you won’t get back the original remote grades or manually 
edited metadata, unless you previously exported them—in which case, you can reimport them and 
apply these in separate steps.
479
Ingest and Organize Media | Chapter 22 Importing and Conforming Timelines
MEDIA

===== Page 480 =====
Duplicate Clips Are Considered 
Separate Sources
In DaVinci Resolve, duplicate clips are treated as separate from the original Media Pool or Timeline 
clips you duplicated them from.
For example, if you import five clips into Media Pool Bin 1, edit them into a timeline, then drag those 
timeline clips into Media Pool Bin 2, the clips in Bin 1 and Bin 2 would not be intrinsically linked.
This means that if you select the original clips in Bin 1 and choose Unlink Selected Clips, any 
instances of those clips used in the timeline will be unlinked—but the duplicate clips in Bin 2 would be 
unaffected.
Summary of Methods for 
Conforming and Relinking
Because timelines, source media and Media Pool clips are managed autonomously, there are 
several methods for conforming and relinking media. The most appropriate method depends on your 
chosen workflow.
	 Conforming clips during XML and AAF import: When importing a project via AAF or XML, 
you can use the embedded file paths to import referenced media into the Media Pool and 
automatically reconform the clips in the imported timeline. If the original media has been moved, 
DaVinci Resolve will prompt you to locate it. Alternatively, you can ignore the AAF or XML file’s 
embedded file paths and instead conform the timeline using different media files that share the 
same file names and timecode.
	 Importing clips before importing an EDL, AAF, or XML: For EDL workflows, you must import 
the media before the EDL itself. The same approach applies to AAF and XML import workflows. 
When you import clips into the Media Pool before importing an AAF or XML, DaVinci Resolve 
automatically reconforms the clips in the imported timeline to those in the Media Pool first. It then 
identifies the media on disk for missing clips. This behavior depends on the options selected in 
the Import AAF/EDL/XML dialog.
	 Conforming missing clips by importing their source media into the Media Pool: When the 
“Automatically conform missing clips added to Media Pool” setting is enabled in the Project 
Settings > General Options panel, DaVinci Resolve automatically matches newly added Media 
Pool clips with missing clips in your project timelines. This applies whether you add clips to the 
Media Pool by importing, copying and pasting, or creating duplicates. For example, importing 
a clip with a matching file name and timecode into the Media Pool can automatically restore a 
missing timeline clip. This setting must be disabled if you use collaborative workflows.
	 Using the Import Additional Clips commands: You can automate the process of importing media 
for missing clips in a timeline. Simply right-click a timeline in the Media Pool and go to Timelines 
> Import > Additional Clips With Loose Filename Match or Additional Clips With Tight Filename 
Match. This searches the selected directory and its subfolders for media that matches the offline 
clips in that timeline. The Loose Filename Match command ignores file extensions and lets you 
conform to alternate media formats, while the Tight Filename Match command requires file 
extensions to match.
	 Reconforming online clips by importing new media into the Media Pool: When the “Automatically 
conform missing clips added to Media Pool” setting is enabled in the Project Settings > General 
Options panel, DaVinci Resolve attempts to update the conformed relationship between the clips 
you’re adding to the Media Pool, and the clips whose Conform Lock Enabled setting has been 
480
Ingest and Organize Media | Chapter 22 Importing and Conforming Timelines
MEDIA

===== Page 481 =====
disabled. This applies whether you add clips to the Media Pool by importing, copying and pasting, 
or creating duplicates.
By default, clips in imported or new timelines have Conform Lock Enabled turned on (unless the 
source media goes missing). This option means that a particular clip in a timeline will only consider 
the source clip in the Media Pool to which it’s currently conformed as the correct match. All other 
clips are ignored, regardless of matching file names and overlapping timecode.
If you right-click a clip in the timeline that has multiple potential matches in the Media Pool, then 
disable Conform Lock Enabled, a “clip conflict” icon appears, with a red <!> badge beside its 
name. Double-click the indicator to view all matching Media Pool clips, from which you can choose 
your desired source.
NOTE: The “Auto conform clips with media added into Media Pool” setting must be 
disabled if you use collaborative workflow.
	 Using Conform Lock commands to force a timeline clip to conform itself to a clip in the Media 
Pool: A manual command that conforms a selected timeline clip to a selected Media Pool clip. It’s 
useful when none of the automatic conforming methods don’t produce the desired result.
	 Using the Relink command on clips or bins in the Media Pool: If there are unlinked clips in the 
Media Pool of your project, use the Relink Media, Relink Selected Clips, or Relink Clips in Selected 
Bins commands to relink clips to the corresponding source media on whatever storage volume it’s 
on. At the same time, any timeline instances of those clips are automatically updated. You can also 
use these commands to force clips to relink to alternative media. The Relink command searches 
all subfolders in the selected directory, making it useful when your media has moved. Note that if 
you’re searching large SAN volumes, choosing a directory that’s too high in the folder hierarchy 
may result in longer search times.
	 Using the Change Source Folder command: This command updates the directory structure of 
each selected clip’s file path into a new file path, based on the parent directory you select. It’s 
useful when media has been moved, but retains its original subdirectory structure. This makes it a 
safe and fast command to use when relinking to a structured collection of media on a SAN volume.
	 Using the Reconform From Bin(s) command: If you have multiple versions of the same clips (with 
identical file names, overlapping timecode, or other matching criteria) separate Media Pool bins, 
you can disable Conform Lock Enabled for every clip in a timeline you want to reconform—then 
use the Reconform From Bin(s) command to reconform timeline clips to Media Pool clips in one or 
more specific bins. You can also choose the matching criteria used during reconforming. DaVinci 
Resolve will only reconform timeline clips that can be matched to media in your chosen bins; 
timeline clips without a match remain unchanged.
	 Using the Reconform From Media Storage command: This command reconforms timeline clips 
directly to media located in a selected file-system directory that hasn’t been imported into the 
Media Pool. You can also choose the specific criteria used during reconforming to match timeline 
clips with clips in the selected bins. Only clips with a valid match are updated, while timeline clips 
without a match remain unchanged.
	 Overwriting clips on disk that are linked to in a DaVinci Resolve project: When a media file has 
been overwritten on disk, DaVinci Resolve automatically updates relinked clips—provided the 
replacement clip has the same file name, timecode, and reel name (if used).
The following sections detail each of these methods of conforming and relinking media.

Conform Multiple Selected Timelines
To conform multiple timelines from the same source media simultaneously, simply select the timelines 
you wish to conform in the Media Pool by Option-clicking or Shift-clicking them. Right-click on one of 
the selected timelines, then select Timelines Reconform from Bins or Reconform from Media Storage.
Unlinking Clips
To unlink media pool clips, select the clip(s) to unlink, right-click any of them, then choose 
Unlink Selected Clips.
Conforming Clips During 
XML and AAF Import
For AAF and XML workflows where DaVinci Resolve relinks imported clips to media on disk or 
reconforms them to clips already in the Media Pool, the clip metadata used for reconforming depends 
on two settings in the Load AAF or XML dialog: “Automatically import source clips into media pool”, 
and “Ignore file extensions when matching”.
The most important settings for conformingmedia in the Load dialog
These two checkboxes interact in a complex manner to let you decide how media is conformed to an 
imported AAF or XML file. Here are the rules:
When Importing Clips With File Extensions Matching Those in the AAF or XML File
Turn “Automatically Import” on and “Ignore file extensions” off.
This default setting is useful when the AAF or XML file you’re importing has references to media you 
want to add to the Media Pool for use.
	 If there are already clips in the Media Pool, DaVinci Resolve will conform as many of them as 
possible by matching the file paths in the AAF or XML file to the stored file paths of each clip 
in the Media Pool. 
	 The software will then import as many remaining missing clips as possible into the Media Pool from 
any storage volumes that are visible to DaVinci Resolve, using the file paths from the XML or AAF.
	 For all remaining clips not found, DaVinci Resolve executes a clip name match in the Media Pool.
	 If there are still missing clips, DaVinci Resolve attempts a timecode match (along with a reel name 
match, if this is enabled) of media pool clips.
	 Finally, for all remaining clips that still aren’t found, you’ll be prompted to manually choose another 
folder to search.

When Importing Clips With Different File Extensions
Turn on both “Automatically import”, and “Ignore file extensions”.
Enabling both these options is useful when the sequence you’re importing was edited using offline 
quality media, and you want to conform to high-quality online media in a different format—possibly in 
the Media Pool, or on another disk. 
For example, if you’ve edited using QuickTime proxies and wish to conform the edit back to its original 
camera RAW files for color grading, you should enable both “Automatically import source clips into 
media pool”, and “Ignore file extensions”. This imports and relinks the RAW files in a single operation.
	 If there are already clips in the Media Pool, DaVinci Resolve attempts to conform as many of these 
clips as possible by matching clip names. 
	 For all remaining clips not found, the user is prompted to choose another folder to search, 
and DaVinci Resolve imports as many clips as possible by matching clip names, ignoring file 
extensions.
	 For all remaining clips that still aren’t found, DaVinci Resolve attempts a timecode match (and reel 
name match, if this is enabled in the Project Settings > General Options panel of clips that are 
already within the Media Pool.
	 Finally, if there are still remaining clips not found, the user is prompted to manually choose another 
folder to search.
Turn on both “Automatically import”, and “Link to source camera files”.
The “Link to source camera files” checkbox only appears when you import AAF files. When 
automatically importing media, enabling this option relinks the imported project to the original camera 
source files, which Media Composer/Symphony track using the Source Name metadata in the AAF file.
When You’re Only Relinking to Clips Already in the Media Pool
Turn “Automatically import” off.
Disable the “Automatically Import source clips into media pool” setting when you want to conform an 
imported AAF or XML to clips in the Media Pool. This is most useful if you’ve already imported the 
original camera media—for example, when reconforming an edited AAF or XML to dailies created 
earlier in DaVinci Resolve.
	 If there are already clips in the Media Pool, DaVinci Resolve attempts to conform as many clips as 
possible by matching the file paths in the XML or AAF to the file paths stored for each clip in the 
Media Pool. 
	 For all remaining clips not found, DaVinci Resolve tries a clip name match of clips that are already 
in the Media Pool.
	 For all remaining clips that still aren’t found, DaVinci Resolve attempts a timecode match (and reel 
name match if this is enabled) of clips that are already within the Media Pool. In this case, the file 
name is not used.
Beware When Choosing a Volume or Folder to Search
When prompted to choose a folder to search, you can optionally choose an entire volume. DaVinci 
Resolve always searches through all subdirectories, and all media on that volume will be found. 
However, the operation time depends on the size and number of files on the selected volume—so you 
can expect long wait times on a SAN volume, for example.

Importing Clips Before Importing 
an EDL, AAF, or XML
When importing media prior to importing an EDL, DaVinci Resolve follows a specific set of rules to 
determine which Media Pool clips correspond to clips in the resulting timeline. These rules also apply 
when you’ve imported media prior to importing an AAF or XML file, and want to prioritize specific 
media over the file paths embedded in those imported timeline formats. 
The following sections elaborate on these rules, and how to use them to your advantage.
Essential Clip Metadata for Easy Conforming and Relinking
When conforming projects in DaVinci Resolve, the accuracy and integrity of clip metadata is critical for 
a successful result. Keep this criteria in mind when preparing your media for use in DaVinci Resolve:
	 Accurate timecode: Each clip requires a valid timecode track, and that timecode should match 
all other instances of that media file within a project. If there are problems with a clip’s timecode, 
you can edit or offset timecode inconsistencies with DaVinci Resolve tools. By default, the “Use 
Timecode” project setting is set to Embedded in the Source Clip—which means that timecode is 
read from the embedded timecode track within a QuickTime or MXF file, or from the header data 
of a DPX frame file. However, you can also enable the “From the source clip frame count” option, 
which lets you read the timecode from the source clip’s frame count for image sequences.
	 File names: When “Assist using reel names from the” in Project Settings > General Options panel 
is disabled (the default setting), DaVinci Resolve conforms clips using file names when importing 
XML and AAF projects. File names can only be only used when conforming XML or AAF files, or 
when importing a DaVinci project. They’re never used when conforming EDLs.
	 Reel Name: This is only used for conforming if “Assist using reel names from the” is enabled in 
Project Settings > General Options panel. Assigning reel names to your media is recommended 
but not essential; it can ease media management for certain operations, especially in EDL 
workflows. However, if you experience problems conforming clips when the “Assist using reel 
names from the” option is enabled, try disabling it.
The way that DaVinci Resolve matches media files to clips in an imported project depends on how 
you’re importing that project.
Defining Clip Metadata When Adding Media to the Media Pool
The rules on defining clip metadata before conforming are different, if your workflow involves any of 
the following: Manually adding media files when editing from scratch in DaVinci Resolve, preparing 
to process dailies, or as a separate step before importing EDL, XML, or AAF project files and 
reconforming them to a higher quality set of media than what was used in the original edit.
	 Timecode: Calculated using the “Timeline Frame Rate” setting in the Project Settings > 
Master Project Settings panel.
	 Reel Names: Determined by enabling or disabling the “Assist using reel names from the” 
checkbox in the Project Settings > General Options panel, and depending on your selected 
option. Reel names can be extracted dynamically, and changing this setting will update your 
Media Pool with the revised reel names. Reel names can also be defined manually if you set 
different methods of reel name extraction per clip.
	 Clip Names: Read and stored, used for AAF and XML imports, but not used for imported EDLs.

How Reel Names Are Identified
The “Assist using reel names from the” checkbox in the Project Settings > General Options panel 
is a crucial setting for controlling the conform process. By default, it’s disabled, and reel names are 
left blank. This is fine for conform workflows that only require the file path or file name and source 
timecode to successfully identify which media files correspond to which clips. 
However, if you need more information to reconform the clips in your project, you can enable the 
“Assist using reel names from the” checkbox, which triggers DaVinci Resolve to use one of four 
methods to automatically define reel names for every clip in the Media Pool.
Automatically Defining Reel Names
When you use the “Assist using reel names from the” options in the Project Settings > General Options 
panel, reel names are extracted dynamically. If you change the method of reel name extraction in the 
project settings, the reel names of all media pool clips will automatically reflect that change. These are 
viewable in the Reel Name column of the Media Pool (when in List view). 
For example, if you change the “Assist using reel names” options from “Source clip file 
pathname” to “Mediapool folder name,” the contents of the Reel Name column are updated. 
This is useful when you’re importing a project for which all clips use the same method of 
determining their reel name.
Manually Choosing Reel Name Definitions for Individual Clips
You can also manually select the criteria for how your media pool clip(s) have their reel names defined, 
using the Clip Attributes dialog. This is useful for project clips that require a different method of reel 
name extraction, or require manually entered reel names.
To manually define reel names for one or more clips:
1	
Select one or more clips in the Media Pool.
2	
Right-click one of the selected clips, and choose Clip Attributes.
3	
Open the Reel Name panel of the Clip Attributes dialog, choose a new option, and click OK.
Once you’ve used Clip Attributes to change the reel names of clips, those clips no longer 
automatically update when you change the “Assist using reel names from the” options in the 
Project Settings > General Options panel. 
For more information on using Clip Attributes, jump to this chapter: Using Clip Metadata.
Methods of Defining Reel Names
There are five options that automatically determine how reel names are extracted from the source 
media when you enable “Assist using reel names from the”. One option is the Clip Attributes Reel 
Name panel, which lets you manually define reel names. The use of reel names is critical in EDL and 
AAF workflows, but less so in XML-centric workflows.
	 Source clip file pathname: Obtains the reel name by extracting it from each media file’s path. This 
means you can extract a reel name from all or part of the file name, or from all or part of the name 
of any folder in the path that encloses that file. This extraction is defined using the Pattern field.
485
Ingest and Organize Media | Chapter 22 Importing and Conforming Timelines
MEDIA

===== Page 486 =====
	 Pattern: A code that defines how a reel name should be extracted from the source clip pathname. 
More information about creating patterns appears later in this chapter.
	 Mediapool folder name: The reel name is obtained from the name of the bin in the Media Pool 
that encloses that clip. For example, in a stereoscopic workflow, you might want to export offline 
stereo media with the “Left” and “Right” bin names in which they’re organized as reel names. 
Another example would be organizing VFX so that it’s incrementally processed in individually 
named bins, such as “VFX_Tuesday_10-12.”
	 Embedding in source clip file: Useful for file formats where the reel name is embedded within the 
media file itself. Blackmagic RAW and other digital cinema cameras, QuickTime files created by 
Final Cut Pro, and DPX frame files are formats that can contain reel name header data.
	 Source clip filename: If there is no defined reel number, often it’s easy to just use the source 
clip filename.
	 User Defined: This option is only available when you manually alter the Reel Name for one or 
more selected clips in the Media Pool using the Clip Attributes dialog. To customize the reel name, 
choose User Defined.
An additional checkbox is also available in the Project Settings > General Options panel, titled “Extract 
reel names from EDL comments.” This is useful for legacy workflows when you wish to conform an EDL 
exported from Final Cut Pro 7 to camera original R3D media.
Extract reel names from EDL comments: Some media file formats, such as R3D, have their reel names 
obtained from file names that exceed the eight-character limit allowed in a standard EDL. This option 
lets DaVinci Resolve extract reel names from appropriately formatted EDL comments, such as those 
output from Final Cut Pro 7.
Using the Pattern Field
If you’re using the Pattern option to extract the reel name from a clip’s source file pathname, you can 
create a search pattern that triggers DaVinci Resolve to extract the reel name in highly specific ways to 
accommodate more unusual workflows. 
Extraction patterns are interpreted from right to left, deciphering each clip’s file path element by 
element starting with the file name, and then considering each enclosing directory’s name to the 
left. Each extraction pattern has a series of text characters and “wild card” operators in unique 
combinations corresponding to the length and names used in the file path.
Here are a series of search characters that may be used:
Extraction Pattern Operators
?
Looks for matches of any single character. Add as many question marks as 
there are characters you want to match. ?? matches two characters such as 
02, while ???? matches four characters such as 0002.
*
A wildcard that creates matches for any sequence of zero or more characters.
%R
Specifies the reel name’s actual location. Reel names may contain any 
character, but should not contain a directory separator (forward slash). 
%_R
Extracts the reel name and strips out the R3D file name underscores found in 
EDLs from Final Cut Pro 7 or earlier.
%D
Matches any directory name or file name. When this is the last operator in a 
pattern, do not add a forward slash.
/
Used to separate any two operators
486
Ingest and Organize Media | Chapter 22 Importing and Conforming Timelines
MEDIA

===== Page 487 =====
If you’re trying to create a new extraction pattern for a unique workflow, use this test dialog before 
applying them to your project.
To test the extraction path:
1	
Turn on “Assist using reel names from the” and click the Test button next to the current Pattern in 
the Project Settings > General Options panel. The “Specify Reel Extraction Pattern” dialog opens.
2	
Type the extraction patten you want to test into the Pattern field. 
3	
Using your preferred method, locate the file path of the media file that you want to test the 
extraction pattern on, then copy or type it into the Sample Path field. 
4	
Click Test. 
5	
If the reel name that appears below is correct, click Apply to copy the extraction pattern into the 
Pattern field of the Project Settings > General Options panel. If the reel name that appears is 
incorrect, modify the extraction pattern and try again.
Examples of Reel Name Extraction Patterns
To better understand how this process works, the following examples show the various methods of 
reel name extraction. The “/” is used as a separator between control parameters.
Example 1: 
This example shows the reel name stored within the parent folder name of the clip.
	 Pattern: */%R/%D
	 File path: vol0/MyMovie/Scans/004B/Frame[1000-2000].dpx
	 Reel name: 004B
Parsing starts from right to left. To analyze this pattern, start from the right. In this case, the %D 
matches the file name FrameNNNN.dpx, where NNNN is the frame number in each file of the clip. 
Moving to the left of the file name, the /%R/ section of the string specifies that the reel name will 
be the entire name of the parent directory immediately above the file. Finally, the * at the start of 
the string says to match any pathname in front of the directory name that has the reel name. This 
string will find the parent directory, regardless of how many levels deep it is nested within the 
directory path.
Example 2: 
Here, the reel name is stored in the parent folder name of the clip and prefixed with the reel name.
	 Pattern: */????%R/%D or alternatively */Reel%R/%D
	 File path: /vol0/MyMovie/Scans/Reel1234/Frame[1000-2000].dpx
	 Reel name: 1234
In this example, both extraction patterns produce the same result. They are also similar to the first 
example. The reel name is still in the parent directory name, but in this case, the fixed characters 
“Reel” are prefixed before the reel name. The first pattern with ???? would match any 4 characters 
in front of the reel name. The second pattern is more specific, and would only match the word 
“Reel” in the directory name.
487
Ingest and Organize Media | Chapter 22 Importing and Conforming Timelines
MEDIA

===== Page 488 =====
Example 3: 
This example shows the reel name stored within the parent folder name two directory levels up.
	 Pattern: */%R/%D/%D
	 File path: /vol0/MyMovie/Scans/004B/134500-135000/Frame[1000-2000].dpx
	 Reel name: 004B
This example is again similar to Example 1—but a key difference is that the reel name is the 
directory name two levels above the clip (versus one level up, in Example 1). 
Example 4: 
Finally, we see the reel name that is embedded within the clip name of the material.
	 Pattern: */Reel%R_*
	 File path: /vol0/MyMovie/Scans/Reel004B_[1000-2000].dpx
	 Reel name: 004B
This example shows a method for extracting the reel name from the file name of the clip. Again, 
starting from the right, the two pattern characters _* match any series of characters, up to the first 
_ character. In this case, it picks up the file extension (.dpx) and the frame number portion of the 
file name. Next, the /Reel%R characters indicate the reel name is the characters between the /
Reel and _ character. The * at the beginning of the pattern will match a file path any number of 
directories deep in front of the file name.
Conform Missing Clips by 
Importing Their Source Media
If your timeline has one or more missing clips, the relationship between that clip in the timeline and the 
Media Pool has been lost. If you manually import clips into the Media Pool that correspond to those 
missing clips, your next steps are determined when you go to Project Settings > General Options 
panel and enable “Automatically conform missing clips added to Media Pool”. If you use collaborative 
workflow, this setting must be disabled.
If you enable the “Auto conform clips with media added into Media Pool” setting when importing 
additional clips, DaVinci Resolve updates the conformed relationship between clips that you add to 
the Media Pool, and missing clips in the various timelines of your project. At the same time, it also 
updates the conform relationship of all other timeline clips that have disabled the Conform Lock 
Enabled option.
If you disable the “Auto conform clips with media added into Media Pool” setting when importing 
additional clips, DaVinci Resolve will not attempt to reconform anything automatically. Instead, it relies 
on you to manually reconform offline or missing clips. Some methods you could use are Reconform 
From Bins, or Conform Lock With Media Pool Clip.
For more information on manually adding clips to the Media Pool, jump to this chapter:  
Adding and Organizing Media with the Media Pool.

If there are many missing clips in the timeline and no corresponding Media Pool clips, one easy fix is to 
automate the process of gathering a list of what’s missing, so that you can import and conform missing 
clips at once. This only works for missing clips, and not unlinked clips. (In the latter case, use the Relink

The conformed Timeline with missing clips.

===== Page 490 =====
Using Conform Lock As a Command
If an unlinked clip in a timeline won’t conform to a clip in the Media Pool even though it’s there, use the 
Conform Lock with Media Pool Clip command. This forces a clip in the timeline to conform to a clip in 
the Media Pool of your choosing. It also automatically suspends the Conform Lock Enabled setting of 
a target clip, ignoring file names and reel names, in favor of conforming the target clip to your manually 
selected clip. At the same time, the timecode is still used to align the clip being conformed with the 
original clip in the timeline.
To conform lock a clip in the Timeline to another clip in the Media Pool:
1	
Select a clip in the Media Pool. For the Force Reconform command to be successful, the clip must 
be equal in length or longer than the selected clip in the Timeline.
2	
Right-click an unconformed clip in the timeline, and choose Conform Lock with Media Pool Clip. 
This conforms the clip you selected in the Media Pool to the selected clip in the Timeline:
If the selected Media Pool clip has timecode matching the selected Timeline clip: The new clip 
is perfectly conformed to match the original clip.
If the selected Media Pool clip doesn’t have timecode matching the selected Timeline clip: The 
new clip is conformed such that the first frame of the Media Pool clip is aligned with the first frame 
of the reconformed clip in the Timeline, and occupies the same duration.
3	
If you right-click that clip again, you’ll see that Conform Lock Enabled is enabled, showing you that 
the clip has successfully conformed to media for which it wasn’t originally a match.
Relinking Clips to Media Files on Disk
The best method for relinking clips in your project that have either gone offline or are not properly 
linked is to use either the Relink Media or Relink selected clips command. Note, the Relink command 
only works for unlinked clips, and not missing clips—since the latter would not have corresponding 
clips in the Media Pool. 
The Relink command is the most flexible method of relinking the Media Pool clips from your project 
with clips in a file system directory of your choice, using file name and timecode as the primary criteria 
for re-creating the correspondence between each clip and its corresponding media file on disk. This 
command is useful for relinking media that’s been moved to another location, or reorganized using 
another file structure on disk.
To relink all unlinked media:
1	
Select the orange Relink icon in the page’s Media Pool.
2	
Select the Locate button next to the specific volume(s) that are missing, and choose a directory 
where the missing files are located.
3	
If the quick search initiated by the Locate buttons doesn’t find the media (even though you know 
it’s there), you can initialize an exhaustive deep disk search for the media by clicking on the Disk 
Search button.
4	
If there are still other clips that can’t be found, you’re prompted to either choose another directory 
altogether to continue searching, or quit.
To relink selected clips:
1	
Select one or more offline clips to relink, or select a bin in the Media Pool bin list that contains 
clips you want to relink, then right-click one of the selected clips or the selected bin, and choose 
Relink Selected Clips from the contextual menu.
490

===== Page 491 =====
2	
When the Relink File dialog opens, choose a directory to look for the files you want to relink 
to, and click OK. DaVinci Resolve attempts to find every clip with a matching file name in the 
subdirectories of this directory, using the original file paths of the clips being relinked. By first 
looking for the clips in their originally located directories, relinking can be quite fast.
3	
If there are clips that couldn’t be found in Step 2, you’re prompted with the option to do a “deep 
search”. If you click Yes, then DaVinci Resolve will look for each clip inside every subdirectory of 
the directory you selected in Step 2. This may take significantly longer, but should be successful 
so long as the media that’s required is within the selected directory structure.
4	
If there are still other clips that can’t be found, you’re prompted to either choose another directory 
altogether to continue searching, or quit.
Using “Change Source Folder” 
to Relink Clips
If you’ve used your file system to move media that’s associated with a DaVinci Resolve project—but 
haven’t changed the directory structure with which it’s organized—you can use the Change Source 
Folder command to quickly relink selected clips in the Media Pool to the new file path of the media on 
disk, using the original file paths as a guide. This is a good relinking method for projects on a SAN. It 
also avoids the long search times that sometimes result from using the Relink command to examine a 
nested hierarchy of folders in a more flexible way.
To relink your Media Pool clips to a new location:
1	
Select your clip(s) in the Media Pool, then right-click one of the selected clips, and choose Change 
Source Folder. The Relink Media window will now display the original path for the material, with 
controls for choosing a new directory.
2	
To the right of the Change To field, click Browse, then use the file navigation dialog to find the new 
location of the media file. Select it and click Open.
3	
If you succeeded in finding the appropriate media file, click Change. Otherwise, click Cancel.
Using the “Reconform From Bins” 
Command
The Reconform From Bins command lets you simultaneously reconform multiple clips in a timeline 
to a specific bin (or bins) of clips with matching metadata. To use this command, select the clips you 
want to reconform in a timeline and disable Conform Lock Enabled. Then use the Reconform From Bin 
command to manually choose another bin of clips in the Media Pool that you want to reconform to.
An important aspect of the Reconform From Bins command is that DaVinci Resolve only reconforms 
timeline clips that can be matched to source clips in selected Media Pool bins. All timeline clips that 
cannot be matched are left as is. This makes the command ideal for when you’ve imported a subset of 
clips to the Media Pool that you need to reconform to clips found throughout an existing timeline. 
For example, you could use this method to:
	 Replace transcoded versions of clips in a timeline with the original camera raw clips.
	 Replace the previous versions of VFX clips in a timeline with new versions.
	 Replace the offline-quality media you’ve been working with so far with online-quality media.
	 Replace your temp clips with rescanned or recaptured stock footage.
491
Ingest and Organize Media | Chapter 22 Importing and Conforming Timelines
MEDIA

===== Page 492 =====
Before using Reconform From Bins, ensure your clips are well-organized in the Media Pool. Ideally, 
they should be in a self-contained bin, or bins separate from the other media used by that timeline. It 
can be a sub-bin, but it must be separate. 
Here’s a simple example: If the media you edited or originally imported is in Bin 1, then import the 
updated versions of all clips that need to be reconformed into Bin 2. Using Reconform From Bins, you 
can now decide which bin your timeline clips should be conformed to—because only timeline clips for 
which there is a valid match are reconformed, while all other timeline clips are ignored. 
DaVinci Resolve lets you choose custom conform options to control which metadata is used when 
matching timeline clips to source clips in the Media Pool. This means you aren’t restricted to only 
using Timecode, Reel Name, and File Name. You could also use any combination of Total Duration, 
Resolution, Bit Depth, Frame Rate, File Format, Codec, and/or Media UMID/UID to control how clips 
are conformed, depending on your needs and what you’re solving for.
The Reconform from Bins dialog
However, if your selected criteria doesn’t match, the Reconform From Bins operation will fail. You can 
either try again with other conform criteria, or manually replace the necessary clips in the Timeline.
Here’s a step-by-step workflow:
To reconform a timeline to clips within a specific Media Pool bin:
1	
Go to the Timeline you want to reconform, and double-click to open it.
2	
Either individually select the specific clips for reconforming, or—to select and reconform all clips in 
the timeline—press Command-A.
3	
Right-click one of the selected clips, and disable Conform Lock Enabled. Repeat this step for all the 
clips you want to reconform. This helps DaVinci Resolve to consider all possible conform matches, 
particularly in cases where there may be multiple clips with overlapping timecode in the Media Pool.
4	
Right-click the current Timeline in the Media Pool, and choose Timelines > Reconform From Bins. 
The Conform Options dialog appears, with Timeline Options and Choose Conform Bins list to the 
left, and the Conform Options panel to the right.

Using Reconform From Media Storage
Starting in version 14, DaVinci Resolve introduced another reconform method that lets you conform 
clips in a timeline to clips in a specific File System directory (including all subdirectories) using the 
Reconform From Media Storage Folders command. This means you can simultaneously reconform 
multiple clips in a timeline to matching source media files on disk without first importing those clips 
to the Media Pool. All clips that can be conformed according to the specified conform criteria will be 
automatically imported as necessary.
An important aspect of the Reconform From Media Storage command is that DaVinci Resolve will 
reconform all timeline clips that can be matched to source media files on disk in the selected Media 
Storage directories, but all Timeline clips that cannot be matched are left as is. This makes Reconform 
From Media Storage an ideal command in the following situations:
	 When you need to reconform clips that are found throughout an existing timeline to a smaller 
subset of media in a specific directory on disk, such as updated VFX or motion graphics from a 
third-party application. 
	 When you need to quickly reconform missing timeline clips throughout an imported timeline, 
and especially when you need to use custom conform criteria to successfully reconform those 
clips. (Unlinked clips can only be reconformed with this command if you select them and disable 
Conform Lock Enabled.)
Similar to the Reconform From Bins command, you can specify the combination of conform criteria 
you want to use to match clips in the timeline with clips in the Media Pool. This means you aren’t 
restricted to only using Timecode, Reel Name, and File Name. You could also use any combination 
of Total Duration, Resolution, Bit Depth, Frame Rate, File Format, Codec, and/or Media UMID/UID 
to control how clips are conformed, depending on your needs and what you’re solving for.

Understanding, Fixing, 
and Using Reel Conflicts
If the Auto conform clips with media added into Media Pool setting is enabled in the Project Settings 
> General Options panel, the same dynamic relationship between clips in the Media Pool and timeline 
are maintained, no matter if they’re linked or unlinked. However, this means if you have two different 
versions of the same clip in the Media Pool, or even two different clips with the same file name (or 
reel name) and the same overlapping timecode, then DaVinci Resolve is capable of automatically 
conforming to either clip. 
Let’s say you have both the camera raw version of a clip, and a ProRes or MXF transcoded version 
imported into the Media Pool at the same time. Both clips share the same content, file name, and 
range of frames. 
These factors could cause a “clip conflict”. You might not notice this at first, since the Conform Lock 
Enabled setting is enabled by default. In this state, all clips in a timeline only consider the current clip in 
the Media Pool to which they’re conformed as the valid clip. In effect, all other clips with file names and 
overlapping timecode that would otherwise make them a valid match are ignored. 
However, if you right-click such a clip in the Timeline and disable Conform Lock Enabled, a “clip 
conflict” icon may appear, indicated by a red <!> conflict icon beside its name in the timeline.
The red <!> conflict icon, indicating at least 
 two clips have matching conform parameters.
Clip conflicts are not always considered an error. They can be a problem if your imported project 
from a separate application contains media that was added with timecode but no reel identifier (for 
example, when shots from multiple unidentified reels all start at 0 hour).
TIP: Overlapping timecode is common in the normal course of work, but should be managed 
by altering each clip’s embedded reel name, or by organizing media in different bins.
497
Ingest and Organize Media | Chapter 22 Importing and Conforming Timelines
MEDIA

===== Page 498 =====
Using Clip Conflicts as a Conform Tool
On the other hand, clip conflicts can be a desirable solution for workflows that require switching 
between versions of a particular clip. If you had an edited timeline comprising of transcoded 
QuickTime versions of camera raw original media, and you only had the transcoded clips in the Media 
Pool, then all is well. 
However, let’s assume that you find yourself in need of the resolution or additional color latitude of 
the camera raw version of a particular clip. If you import the camera raw version of that clip, nothing 
changes. But if you right-click that clip in the Timeline and deselect Conform Lock Enabled, the red 
<!> conflict badge appears beside the clip name in the Timeline. This means the clip in the Timeline 
is accurately seeing the relationship between it and the now two simultaneously named clips with 
timecode overlap in the Media Pool.
The current relationship between this timeline clip and the one to which it is conformed doesn’t 
change; this badge simply indicates there is a second clip in the Media Pool to which you could 
conform this clip in the Timeline. You can now select your preferred clip by double-clicking the badge 
and following the below steps.
Resolving Clip Conflicts
Clip conflicts are easy to resolve. In fact, this feature is the very basis for the name of our software.
To resolve a reel conflict by relinking a clip’s media:
1	
Double-click the red <!> conflict badge beside the clip name in the Timeline.
The Conflict Resolution window appears with a list of files in the Media Pool (of any format) that 
have identical file names or reel names and overlapping timecodes with the clip you right‑clicked. 
Each item in this list has a thumbnail of the clip, the file path of the media on disk, the file name, 
starting timecode, reel name (if any), and creation date. These will help you decide which 
clip to use.
The Conflict Resolution window shows which other clips have overlapping timecode and reel information
498
Ingest and Organize Media | Chapter 22 Importing and Conforming Timelines
MEDIA

===== Page 499 =====
2	
Choose the clip that you want to conform to, then click Apply. The clip in the Timeline now reflects 
your selected media, and the red <!> conflict badge is replaced with a black “resolved” badge. 
To change which Media Pool clip you want to conform to, simply double-click the “resolved” 
badge. It remains a dynamic relationship.
A “resolved” badge shows that the conflict was resolved
Re-editing Media Directly to the Timeline
If none of the above methods work, try replacing the problem clip. For example, you may need to 
replace an old version of an effects shot with a newer one—or replace an offline version of a stock 
footage shot with a higher quality one. The problem occurs when you have a mismatched filename 
and/or timecode, no reel name, and the files are in different formats, frame sizes, and durations. 
In this case, it’s a good thing that DaVinci Resolve has such excellent editing tools. 
When fixing conform problems with manual editing, the replace edit is your friend. For example, you 
could use a replace edit to match a new incoming clip’s timing to the old one. Or you could use a three-
point edit, a place on top edit, or even a simple drag and drop edit to update the clip in the Timeline. 
For information on the different edit types in DaVinci Resolve, jump to this chapter:  
Editing Basics.
How Grades Are Linked 
to Multiple Timelines
If your project uses Remote versions, clips that reference the same file in the Media Pool are linked 
and share their Remote grades. 
For example, two close-up shots clips taken from the same source file will share the same remote 
grades, since they reference the same media. This behavior applies across multiple timelines. If clips in 
different timelines reference the same Media Pool clip, they share the same Remote grades. 
This is why you can grade one timeline, and then import a re-edited version via EDL, AAF, or XML, and 
have the new timeline automatically inherit the existing grades from the previous timeline.
To independently grade a timeline, first select it, then open the Color page > right-click any clip in the 
Thumbnail timeline > choose Copy Remote Grades to Local. All grades are copied to Local versions, 
and changes will only affect that timeline. 
For more information on Local and Remote versions, jump to this chapter: Grade Management.

Creating Digital Dailies 
for Round Trip Workflows
Step 1–Ingest Media and Add/Edit Metadata
You don’t need to export a project file from an NLE before working in DaVinci Resolve. The Media 
Storage browser on the Media page lets you access any available storage volume, and import 
compatible media directly into the Media Pool.
The Media Storage browser with scrubbable clip thumbnails.
The Media Pool is DaVinci Resolve’s project library for all media used in the current project. You 
can organize clips in into multiple bins, and use the Metadata Editor to add descriptions, notes, 
scene and take information, flags, shooting days and dates, program and episode details, and

The Media Pool.

Step 2–Sync Audio to the Dailies
If your video format contains embedded audio, DaVinci Resolve can pass that audio through when 
rendering from the Deliver page. If your production uses dual-system audio recording, there are 
various ways to sync it in the Media page.
You can also import timecoded Broadcast WAV. files into the same bin as the accompanying video 
clips—or into a sub-bin, if preferred—before syncing the dailies in DaVinci Resolve. Once you’ve 
imported the video and audio media you want to sync into the Media Pool of the Media page, 
right-click the enclosing folder and choose Auto-Sync Audio Based on Timecode. This syncs every 
timecode-matched pair of audio and video media clips within the same folder. Alternatively, to add the 
synced audio tracks to audio tracks already present in the video clips, choose Auto-Sync Audio Based 
on Timecode and Append Tracks.
TIP: For the best results, use different folders for each day’s audio and video clips.
If you don’t have synced timecode, but your video clips contain separately recorded audio (e.g. via 
an on-camera microphone) that matches the dual-system audio recordings, you can instead use 
waveform syncing. 
Import your separately recorded audio files into the same bin as the accompanying video clips, or into 
a sub-bin. Then right-click the enclosing folder and choose Auto-Sync Audio Based on Waveform. 
This syncs every timecode-matched pair of audio and video media clips within the same folder. 
Alternatively, to add the synced audio tracks to any audio tracks already present in the video clips, 
choose Auto-Sync Audio Based on Waveform and Append Tracks.
TIP: For the best and quickest results during waveform syncing, use different folders for each 
day’s audio and video clips—or even different folders per scene. This reduces the number of 
waveforms that need to be compared each time.
Open the video clip in the Media page viewer, click the Waveform button in the Audio panel, then 
select the corresponding audio clip to display its waveform. Position the Viewer and Audio panel 
playheads on the matching sync points, then click the Audio panel’s Link button to lock the audio and 
video together.
If neither timecode nor waveform matching is available, you can manually sync audio using a 
clapboard or any other visual sync point. Select a video clip to open in the Media page viewer, 
click the Waveform button in the Audio panel, then select the corresponding audio clip to display 
its waveform in the audio panel. From here, you can drag the Viewer and Audio panel’s playheads 
to the video and audio sync points, and click the Audio panel’s Link button to lock the audio and 
video together.
For more information on syncing audio and video in the Edit page, jump to this chapter: 
Modifying Clips and Clip Attributes.
