MEDIA

===== Page 562 =====
4	
When you’re done, click OK.
Timecode cannot be a negative value, so don’t set the start frame to zero. Another common 
organizational technique is to change the hour number whenever you change rolls, to coincide 
with the film roll’s number, which makes it easy to identify a scanned clip with the corresponding 
source roll and frame range.
Your Cintel Scanner has built in ‘Options Interface’ ports for adding optional hardware in the future. 
This offers the ability to add optional features such as reading KeyKode from the camera negative, 
or optical/magnetic audio. 
For more information, see the ‘Optional Audio and KeyKode Reader’ section in the Blackmagic 
Cintel manual .
Choose a Location to Save the Scanned Frames
Once all this is done, scroll down to the ‘capture info’ controls in DaVinci Resolve’s film scanner panel, 
and click the ‘browse’ button to choose a location for the scanned files. You can use the other fields 
in this section to set what prefix you want to add to the name of the scanned files and enclosing 
folders. The ‘file name prefix’ updates the file name preview that’s shown at the top in the header. The 
header also shows the file path, resolution, frame rate, duration, and the format. Specify what roll, reel, 
clip, and program information you want associated with the scanned media. The ‘timestamp prefix’ 
checkbox in the ‘Capture info’ controls is selected by default and will save your clips to independent 
sub-folders within the destination folder, together with a timecode prefix in the file name.
If you want to save all your clips together in one master destination folder, simply deselect 
the checkbox.
When you capture an HDR clip, the scanner completes a high exposure scan and saves it in a hidden 
folder named .HDR inside the same folder as the standard scan. If you delete the .HDR folder, the scan 
converts to a normal clip after refreshing it in the media storage and re-importing the clip into media 
pool. This is useful if there is a problem with the HDR portion of the scan, as you can easily convert it 
to a regular CRI clip. 
Check the Codec
DaVinci Resolve selects the ‘Cintel Raw’ codec by default, or you can choose ‘Cintel Raw 3:1’.
The Cintel Raw Format
The Cintel Raw Format Bayer pattern of each film frame scanned with your Cintel scanner’s 
sensor is saved with embedded scanner metadata as a 12-bit linear Cintel Raw Image, or CRI, 
image sequence. When grading in DaVinci Resolve, CRI images are automatically debayered 
as 12-bit log encoded image data.
The logarithmic encoding is similar, but not identical to Cineon encoding. For example, 
negative film is encoded using a Gamma of 2.046 for density, while print film is encoded 
using a full range Gamma 2.2 curve to ensure that no image data is clipped. Both of these 
logarithmic encodings can be converted to a linear color space using the ‘Cintel to Linear’ 
1D LUT, before converting to other color spaces you may want to work in.
The film is scanned using the full sensor area of 4096x3072 to keep the audio waveform 
visible for optical audio and to accommodate perforation visibility for stabilization. The image 
is then cropped and the resolution of the capture files depends on the source film format 
after overscan for perforations and the audio area are removed. 
562
Ingest and Organize Media | Chapter 25 Capturing From the Cintel Film Scanner
MEDIA

===== Page 563 =====
For more information on scanning resolutions for different types of film, see the 
‘specifications’ section.
The Cintel scanner creates Cintel Raw files with variable bitrate lossless compression by 
default. This is visually lossless compression and achieves approximately 3:2 reduction in file 
size depending on image content. However, Cintel Raw 3:1 uses lossy compression with a 
ratio of approximately 3:1. This is still very high quality but may not always be visually lossless. 
For example, files for 35mm 4 perf are approximately 12.5MB with Cintel Raw and 
approximately 6.3MB with Cintel Raw 3:1. Files for 16mm are approximately 4MB with 
Cintel Raw and approximately 2MB with Cintel Raw 3:1.
CinemaDNG Quality Settings 
To control the quality of CRI files, use the ‘decode quality’ and ‘play quality’ CinemaDNG settings 
located in the Camera Raw panel of the project Settings. These settings are ‘full’ by default. On 
computers with low processor or memory resources, these settings may be lowered but this will affect 
the quality of the final render.
Set the Timeline Resolution
DaVinci Resolve displays and renders the output from the scanner using the same resolution as the 
timeline. For example, for 35mm 4 perforation film, a custom resolution of 4096x3072 would be 
required for maximum resolution.
NOTE: If your timeline is set for HDR with the desired deliverable at Ultra HD, a loss of 
resolution may occur.
For more information on the cropped image area resolutions for all film gauges, refer to the 
‘effective resolutions’ in the ‘specifications’ section. Alternatively, for the full native resolution 
of the captured clip, access the ‘clips attributes’ in DaVinci Resolve.
Adjusting the Color of the Scanner
DaVinci Resolve’s film scanner panel gives you control over the exposure and color temperature of the 
light used to illuminate the film for scanning. You can adjust these via the light source master wheel 
and RGB controls, in order to maximize the amount of information you’re extracting from each frame, 
while preventing any part of the image from being irretrievably clipped. While it’s true that CRI is a raw 
image format, there’s no latitude beyond the internal data range used by DaVinci, so be mindful that if 
you’re clipping data in the built in video scopes while scanning, it might be clipped permanently in the 
scanned media.
How often you’ll adjust the color and exposure of scanned shots depends on how much variety there 
is in the scenes on a particular film roll. For example, some rolls may have many takes of the same 
scene, all of which have the same lighting and which can share the same adjustments.
Meanwhile, other rolls may have a variety of different scenes with widely different lighting in each one, 
necessitating you to make individual adjustments for each scanned clip to maximize data quality.
563
Ingest and Organize Media | Chapter 25 Capturing From the Cintel Film Scanner
MEDIA

===== Page 564 =====
This is important because the light source master wheel and RGB controls cannot be automatically 
changed between scanned clips in a log and capture workflow. This means that the current light 
source settings will be used for all clips you scan until you manually change those settings again, even 
for clips that you’ve logged from different parts of a film roll. This means that the log and capture style 
of working is only advisable in situations where it makes sense to log multiple clips that share the 
same light source master wheel and RGB control adjustments.
Otherwise, it’s recommended you make lighting adjustments on a clip by clip basis, as you scan each 
clip, in situations where you need maximum image quality for finishing. Keep in mind that the goal for 
these adjustments is to maximize image data from the scan, not to create the final look of the clips, 
which you’ll accomplish later in the grading phase of work using the controls of the ‘color’ page.
To adjust the light source settings, find a typical image for the section of roll or for the first series of 
shots you’re going to scan, and adjust the light source while viewing the built in video scopes.
Adjust the light source master wheel to set the intensity of the light source used to illuminate the film, 
raising or lowering the level of the R, G, and B channels all at once. For a typical camera negative, 
this lets you adjust the black point of the film image. In a negative print, the darkest part of the image 
corresponds to the highlights of the film image. Set the light source master wheel to sit just above 
the typical Dmin value of 95, as measured on the histogram of the video scopes, which guarantees 
that the highlights won’t be clipped by the Cineon LOG conversion that DaVinci uses to debayer the 
CRI image for grading. For positive film, manually adjust the light source levels so that no part of the 
highlights or shadows of the signal is being clipped; typically 1000 in 10-bit or 4000 in 12-bit.
You can turn on ‘show reference levels’ in the waveform, RGB parade, or histogram scopes, and set 
the ‘low’ value to indicate the digital Dmin value of 95.
Once that’s accomplished, adjust the RGB controls to rebalance all three color channels by varying 
amounts to alter the color temperature of the light source used to illuminate the film, to produce the 
most useful, or neutral, color balance in the scanned result.
Scanning One or More Sections of Film
After you’ve adjusted the light source, it’s a good idea to stay organized as you scan each clip by 
entering all relevant metadata into the metadata editor as you go. The ‘capture info’ group of metadata 
fields contains information for defining the file name prefix, roll, reel number, clip number, program 
name, flags, and whether a particular take is good. If you populate these fields before scanning a clip, 
that metadata will be written into the clip.
At the bottom of the ‘capture info’ panel, you will see four buttons for film scanning.
With all of this accomplished, you can scan the film in one of four ways:
	 Capture Now: Use the capture now button to capture long sections of a reel all at once. Clicking 
‘capture now’ begins scanning near the current frame, ending whenever you click ‘stop’.
If ‘Enable 2 Pass HDR Scan’ is selected, click ‘Capture HDR’ after the capture has begun to let 
DaVinci Resolve know you’ve reached the end of your desired clip so it can now proceed to 
capture the high exposure pass. If you scan the entire reel without clicking ‘Capture HDR’, the 
scanner automatically proceeds with the high intensity scan from where you started it until the end 
of the reel.
	 Capture Clip: A more controlled means of scanning specific sections of film. After you’ve used the 
transport controls and the In and Out button to define a section of film, clicking ‘capture clip’ scans 
that one clip and then stops. 
If ‘Enable 2 Pass HDR Scan’ is selected, the high intensity HDR scan uses the same In and Out 
points as the initial scan.

===== Page 565 =====
	 Batch Clips: A way you can log multiple clips in advance of scanning them all at once using the 
current light source settings in DaVinci Resolve’s film scanner panel. Log each clip in advance by 
setting In and Out points for each section of film you want to scan, and click the ‘log clip’ button 
to save that frame range as an unscanned clip in the media pool. When you click ‘batch clips’, 
all unscanned clips will be scanned one after the other until the job is complete. You can also 
select one or more unscanned clips, and only the selected clips will be scanned. Furthermore, 
you can import an EDL that corresponds to a particular film roll, and use the resulting logged 
clips for scanning.
NOTE: When you click the ‘log clip’ button, Cintel Scanner applies the same 
project settings to all clips in the batch, and uses the newest project settings at the 
time of capture. You are advised to confirm the scanner settings before starting the 
batch capture.
If ‘Enable 2 Pass HDR Scan’ is selected, the high intensity HDR scan uses the same sets of In and 
Out points as the initial batch of scans.
For more information on batch capture workflows, jump to this chapter:  
Ingesting From Tape.
	
 Snapshot: Capture a single frame with normal exposure and current scanner settings.
Once scanning, if DaVinci Resolve detects that your storage bandwidth is too low to capture at the 
selected speed, the scan speed will automatically adjust to ensure the capture is successful. If you 
are using the optional Audio and KeyKode Reader accessory, the audio sample rate will also be 
adjusted to maintain your chosen audio quality.
Extracting Audio
If the film you’re scanning also contains an optical sound track, you can extract the audio in a separate 
step. There is a standard image frame to audio frame offset of 26 frames for 16mm and 21 frames for 
35mm that DaVinci automatically aligns when extracting the audio. Select all of the clips that have 
an optical sound track, then right-click one of the selected clips and choose ‘extract audio’. Resolve 
analyzes the overlapping optical track area of each frame and automatically generates a matching 
audio track, synchronized with the scanned image sequence. 
Each clip’s audio will be automatically extracted, embedded in the clip and saved to the same 
directory the scanned frames have been written to. A small audio icon will appear on the corner of 
your clip’s thumbnail so you know there is a corresponding audio file.
You can filter the contents in the media storage to make it easier to manage them.
565
Ingest and Organize Media | Chapter 25 Capturing From the Cintel Film Scanner
MEDIA

===== Page 566 =====
To make extraction easier, you can filter the clips in the media storage by name, resolution, date 
modified or by film clips only. Filtering your clips makes it easier for you to find and select exactly what 
you need. You can also make a large selection and extract audio from multiple clips at once by right 
clicking on your selection and choosing ‘extract audio…’ from the menu. During audio extraction, an 
information box indicates the progress. You can click the ‘stop’ button any time to stop the extraction.
If the ‘timestamp prefix’ checkbox was deselected in the ‘capture info’ section when your clips 
were scanned, and you want to have extracted audio automatically embedded in your clips, always 
remember to extract audio from the clips inside the media pool.
Audio Extraction Settings
Normally, once you have selected the film type, the automatic features in DaVinci Resolve will extract 
your optical audio perfectly. However, the condition of the optical track can vary with the condition of 
the film being loaded and in some instances this can confuse the automation. If this happens, you can 
bypass the automatic features and make adjustments manually.
For manual adjustments, simply open the ‘Audio Extraction’ settings window by clicking 
on ‘Show Cintel Audio Settings’ in the inspector options near the top right of the viewer.
Audio extraction settings let you make the following manual adjustments:
Show audio scan area 
This checkbox turns the audio scan area guides on or off. The guides are displayed as a box on the 
side of the frame covering the optical audio scan area and shows what optical information will be 
used during extraction. The position of the guides will conform to the film type you have selected. 
However, you can change the position manually if you need to. The audio scan area guides are also 
great indicators to show you what is happening during the extraction process so you can identify any 
potential troubles and make manual adjustments.
Inside the box is a thin red line. This line is the mid point detector which detects the separation 
between stereo audio channels. When mono sound is detected during audio extraction, the mid point 
detector disappears and the guides will adjust automatically to suit the width of the mono optical track.

make manual adjustments, if needed.
TIP: If you need a closer inspection of the audio scan area guides, you can zoom into the

of zoom from the sizing options at the top left corner of the viewer, then click and drag the

When ‘show audio scan area’ setting is turned on, the audio area guides will be visible so 
you can see exactly what information is being used and monitor the extraction process.
Override audio scan area 
This setting provides sliders for adjusting the horizontal and vertical positioning, width, and height of 
the audio scan area guides. 
These settings include:
567
Ingest and Organize Media | Chapter 25 Capturing From the Cintel Film Scanner
MEDIA

===== Page 568 =====
	 Left and Width: If your film type is such that audio appears on the right side of the frame, you 
can simply adjust the ‘left’ slider to move the guide box to the right. Normally, this will happen 
automatically if you have the corresponding film type selected, but the setting gives you more 
flexibility for adjustments if you need it. Similarly, the ‘width’ setting is used to adjust the width of 
the scan area.
These are helpful tools for making subtle adjustments to the side edges of the guide box if there 
are unwanted elements inside the film’s optical audio area. This can happen due to perforation 
wear and tear, or varying print qualities, and can sometimes interfere with the quality of the audio 
extraction. You can help avoid this by making a subtle movement to the side edges to keep the 
stray elements outside of the guide box.
	 Top: This setting adjusts the vertical position of the guide box. 
	 Height: Sometimes film frames on older rolls of film may be slightly smaller than normal due 
to shrinkage over time. When making manual adjustments to the guide box, you can make 
adjustments for film shrinkage using the ‘height’ slider.
	 Auto adjust audio scan height: This setting is on by default and automatically adjusts the guide 
box height to align with the audio waveform at the top of each frame. The automatic feature works 
well for normal audio conditions, however, if during extraction you notice the box moving randomly 
and the quality of the extraction is affected, it may be due to similar features in the audio track 
overlapping between frames. If this occurs, deselect the checkbox and try the extraction again.
If deselecting the ‘Auto adjust audio scan height’ checkbox, make sure the ‘height’ setting places 
the guide box at the optimal position for the frame. Making manual adjustments can help if you 
need them, but don’t forget to turn the automatic features back on afterwards!
TIP: If deselecting the ‘Auto adjust audio scan height’ checkbox, make sure the ‘height’ 
setting places the guide box at the optimal position for the frame. Making manual 
adjustments can help if you need them, but don’t forget to turn the automatic features 
back on afterwards!
	 Audio waveform color is white: Depending on the scanned film type, the audio waveform may be 
black or white. If the waveform is white, make sure the corresponding checkbox is enabled. This 
will ensure the white information in the waveform is used during audio extraction. If the waveform 
is black and the surrounding audio area is white, disable the checkbox so DaVinci knows to use 
the black information in the waveform. Other automatic features, such as mid point and mono 
detection, also rely on this setting being set correctly.
	 Override firmware stability: In rare instances, the condition of the film may have created large 
movements in the frame due to the internal firmware stabilization. This can cause the audio 
extraction guide box to misalign with the optical track. If this occurs, enabling ‘override firmware 
stability’ lets the audio extraction guide box track the film perforations independently and adjust 
its positioning for potentially better results.
	 Variable density audio: If your film contains variable density audio, make sure you select the 
‘Variable density audio’ checkbox so DaVinci Resolve knows the type of audio to extract. The 
default state is set to ‘off’ for variable area audio soundtracks. 
If you haven’t used variable density audio before, you can visually identify it as a tight sequence 
of shaded lines, similar to a bar code with the lines squeezed closer together. By comparison, 
‘variable area’ soundtracks appear as an audio waveform.

Color Space and Sizing
A pair of 1D LUTs, ‘Cintel Negative to Linear,’ and ‘Cintel Print to Linear,’ have been provided to help 
you convert scanned media to a color space in which you can do further work. You can apply these 
LUTs via a node in the ‘color’ page to convert the original scans to a Linear color space. However, if 
you want to convert the image to Rec. 709 or to Cineon for further adjustment, you’ll want to apply a 
second LUT in a second node. The default color space for print is a 2.2 gamma standard log curve, 
and all others are 2.046 film density log gamma.
In general for negative film, it’s best to “color invert” after the second LUT is applied. Furthermore, 
normally some grading is required on the Linear data to remove black offsets, due to Dmin, for proper 
conversion into the destination color space. There are a variety of VFX IO LUTs available in the 3D LUT 
submenu of each node’s contextual menu that let you convert an image from Linear color space to any 
other color space you want to work within.
Using three nodes to convert a film scan using LUTs; node 1 
converts from Negative or Print to Linear, node 2 converts from 
Linear to Rec. 709, and node 3, if required, inverts the color
NOTE: Applying a LUT within a node will clip any image data falling below 0 and above 1. 
To prevent clipping, you can use the Lift/Gamma/Gain controls within any node with a LUT 
applied to adjust your image levels prior to the transform applied by the LUT within that node.
The format of the film you’re scanning and the way the material was originally shot both affect the 
framing. You can adjust the final framing of your scanned clip by resizing, zooming, stretching, panning, 
tilting, and more. On the ‘Color’ page, open the ‘Sizing’ palette and use the ‘Input Sizing’ mode to 
create the necessary framing. To save your sizing preferences as a preset, open the menu, select 
‘save as new preset’ and enter a name for your preset.
Once you’ve created an appropriate sizing preset for a given type of media, you can apply that preset 
to multiple film scans all at once, in either the Color page or in the Media Pool using the ‘change input 
sizing preset’ command, found in the contextual menu of selected clips. 
 For more information on sizing, jump to this chapter: Sizing and Image Stabilization
Creating a sizing preset in the Sizing palette of the Color page

The Photo Page
The Photo page is primarily a photo editing application—but with deep integration into the rest of 
DaVinci Resolve’s effects and toolset, it opens up more creative possibilities than still-image editing. 
Using Photo Albums, you can pass full resolution stills into the Cut, Edit, Color, and Fusion pages for 
additional processing.
The Photo Page
The Photo page features a full-image management pipeline including tagging, favorites, ratings, and 
photo album collections. In addition, you can tether your camera to the Photo page, and capture 
images and control your camera settings live. The new IntelliSearch feature helps to analyze your 
images and search for them based on content, objects, people, colors, and more. The Photo page 
includes an extensive, built-in effects library with some of the most powerful Resolve FX and Fusion 
FX ready to use.
With the addition of the Photo page to DaVinci Resolve, you can move fluidly between photos, video 
editing, color grading, VFX and audio post, all in real time.
The Interface Toolbar
At the very top of the Photo page is a toolbar with buttons that let you show or hide different parts of 
the user interface. These buttons are as follows, from left to right:
The Photo Page Toolbar.
Media Pool: Opens or hides a smaller version of the full Media Pool page, allowing 
access to all the images used in the project.
Effects Library: Opens or hides the repository of all transitions, generators, and effects 
that are available for use in the Photo page.

effects clips. These are hidden from view, as the Photo Page is dedicated to just still images.

Photo Albums
This tab opens up the Photo Album at the bottom of the interface. Like their physical analog, 
Photo Albums in the Photo page are where you store and organize collections of still images. 
In DaVinci Resolve, you can equate them to a special type of timeline, built from user-curated stills.
To maximize the still photo capabilities in DaVinci Resolve 21, it’s crucial that you organize your media 
pool images into photo albums. Photos are resolution- and frame rate-independent, while timelines 
are not. The Photo page uses the Photo Album as its central organizational container, and allows your 
photos to interact with the rest of the pages in DaVinci Resolve.

In the Photo page, the Metadata Editor opens in the same place as the Inspector. When you select

uneditable information about the selected clip, including the file name, directory, duration, frame rate, 
resolution, and codec.

	 Metadata Presets (to the left): This is your default option. If you’ve used the Metadata panel of

The heart of the Metadata Editor is a series of editable fields underneath the header that let you

The Media Pool
In the Photo page, your Media Pool contains all the still image media that you’ve imported for editing 
into the current project—as well as all the albums that you’ll use to organize your photos. 
Unlike the media pools found on other pages, your view is limited to still images only. This means it 
won’t show any video, audio, timelines, or effects clips.
The Media Pool in the Photo Page
The Media Pool Toolbar
The top toolbar in the Media Pool includes a toolset for importing and organizing your photos.
The Media Pool toolbar in the Photo page
Bin List: Clicking this icon opens the bin hierarchy (all bins and sub-bins) for the 
selected project. Clicking on a bin name opens that bin in the Media Pool.
Back/Forward: Clicking on these arrows takes you backwards or forwards in the 
bin history.
Import Media: Imports images using your file browser.

Cloud folder.

Bin List
When you click on the Bin List in the upper left, you can view a hierarchical list of bins used for

a single bin named “Master,” but you can add more bins to organize timelines and clips by clicking on 
the Bin List and choosing + Add Bin. You can rename any custom bin by double-clicking on its name 
and typing a new one, or by right-clicking a bin’s name and choosing Rename Bin. 
The browser area shows the contents of your currently selected folder. Every still photo, bin, and 
album appears here. You can create an unlimited number of albums within a single project.
The Media Pool can be displayed in either Thumbnail view, or List view. 
In List view, you can sort the contents by any subset of all the metadata available in the Metadata

Bins and Smart Bins
There are two kinds of bins in the Media Pool, and each appears in its own section of the Bin List. 
These are the differences between both bins:
	 Bins: Simple, manually populated folders. Drag and drop anything you like into a bin—you can also 
relocate your media to another bin at any time. Bins may be hierarchically organized, so you can 
create a matryoshka nesting doll of bins, if you’d like. To create a new bin, right-click within the bin 
list and choose Add Bin from the contextual menu.
	 Smart Bins: These are procedurally populated bins, meaning that the custom rules employing 
metadata are used to dynamically filter the contents of the Media Pool whenever you select 
a Smart Bin. In effect, Smart Bins help to organize the contents of your project—including the 
metadata attached to each photo, from exif data and description text to keywords and comments. 
This allows for the quicker retrieval of specific photos when you need them. To create a new Smart 
Bin, click the bin list and choose + Add Smart Bin. In the dialog box that appears, you can edit the 
name of that bin and the rules it uses to filter clips. 
	 Then click Create Smart Bin.

Metadata
When you go to the Photo page and click on the Metadata tab, the Metadata Editor opens in the same 
place as the Inspector. Selecting a photo in the Media Pool or Album displays its metadata within 
the editor. If you select multiple clips, only the first clip’s information appears. The Metadata Editor’s 
header contains uneditable information about the selected clip—including the file name, directory, 
duration, frame rate, resolution, and codec.
To choose which set of metadata is displayed in the Metadata Editor, navigate to the two dropdown 
menus located at the top.
	 Metadata Presets (to the left): By default, this is set to “Default”. If you’ve used the Metadata panel 
of the User Preferences to create your own custom sets of metadata, you can use this dropdown 
to choose which one to expose.
	 Metadata Groups (to the right): This dropdown menu lets you switch between the various groups 
of metadata that are available, grouped for specific tasks or workflows.
At the heart of the Metadata Editor is a series of editable fields beneath the header that let you 
review and edit the various metadata parameters that are available. For example, in the Camera 
metadata group, you can manually adjust EXIF data such as shutter speed, ISO, lens type, 
and so on.
The Metadata tab, opened to the Camera Metadata group. Here you 
can edit fields including ISO, shutter speed, aperture, and more.

Understanding Photo Albums
To get the most out of DaVinci Resolve’s still-photo capabilities, organizing your media pool images 
into Photo Albums is a must. Photo Albums are generally analogous to timelines in the other pages of 
DaVinci Resolve, but with two major differences:
	 Photo Albums are independent of both resolution and frame rate.
	 Timelines have a set resolution and frame rate.
The Photo page uses the Photo Album as its central organizational container, and determines how 
your photos will interact with the other pages in DaVinci Resolve. 
The Photo Album translates the single-frame nature of still images into a format that can be used 
within DaVinci Resolve’s timeline-based workflow.
Photo Album
This tab opens up the Photo Album at the bottom of the interface. Like their physical analog, 
Photo Albums in the Photo page are where you store and organize collections of still images, and any 
adjustments or changes that you’ve made to the image. In DaVinci Resolve, you can equate them to a 
special type of timeline, built from user-curated stills.
You can create an unlimited number of photo albums to organize your stills.
The Photo Album interface
A Photo Album in the Media Pool
To create a Photo Album:
	 Right-click in the Media Pool and select New Photo Album from the context menu.
	 In the main menu, select File > New Photo Album.
To add an image or images to a Photo Album:
1	
Select an image or group of images in the Media Pool.
2	
Right-click on an image and select Add Photo(s) to Album
3	
The selected photos will be added to the current Photo Album 
To delete an image or images from a Photo Album:
1	
Select an image or group of images in the Media Pool.
2	
Right-click on an image and choose Delete Selected.
3	
The selected photos will be removed from the current Photo Album.

Using the Same Photo in Multiple Albums
You can add the same photo to multiple albums, but any adjustments you make to that photo will 
be applied across all the albums it’s located in. This means the same photo cannot be adjusted 
independently, as long as you’re in the same project.
Filtering a Photo Album
Once an album has been created and populated, you can use the Photo Album toolset to organize, 
sort and label still images for further use in DaVinci Resolve. You can add flags, colors, and tags to 
images in the Viewer, then use the filter tools in the Photo Album to organize and sort them.
NOTE: You cannot rearrange the order of your photos in an photo album manually by 
dragging them like you would in a timeline. Unlike a video timeline, there is no “before” 
or “after” in a photo album. You can modify their sequence by filtering the album, as 
described below.
The Photo Album filtering icons
Filtering a photo album:
The filter icons generally have a click, and right-click function that work in tandem. The icons will 
highlight white if they’re active.
	 Filters: Toggle this switch to turn on or off all of the filters below. 
Tags: Click on this icon to filter the photos in the album based on tags. 
Right‑click on the icon to choose the criteria by Good Take, Untagged, or 
Rejected flags, or a combination of those tags.
Rating: Click on this icon to filter the photos in the album based on rating. 
Right‑click on the icon to choose the criteria—this includes equal to, is less than 
or equal to, and is more than or equal to. Then add the star rating you want to 
use as the base criteria.
Flags: Click on this icon to filter the photos in the album based on flags. 
Right-click on the icon to choose which color flag or flags you want to use as 
the criteria.
Color: Click on this icon to filter the photos in the album based on clip color. 
Right-click on the icon to choose which color or colors you want to use as 
the criteria.

Advanced Filtering
For more advanced filtering options, you can sort and filter photos using the dropdown menu beside 
the Photo Album tag. 
Click on the Photo Album dropdown menu (circled red) 
to view the advanced filtering options
You can filter a photo album by the following attributes:
	 Sort By: Opens the standard sorting criteria that is also found in the filter header of 
the Photo Album.
	 All Photos: No photos are filtered, and every image in the current album is shown.
	 Selected Photos: Filters all currently selected photos.
	 Graded Photos: Filters all photos that have been adjusted or graded.
	 Ungraded Photos: Filters all photos that have not been adjusted or graded.
	 Modified Photos: Filters all photos by the most recent time they were modified. 
A submenu selects a time boundary for the filter (last hour, last 3 hours etc.). 
	 People: Filters photos by the individual humans in them, as analyzed by IntelliSearch.
	 Grouped: Filters all photos belonging to a particular group, a submenu shows all available groups.
	 HDR Graded: Filters photos based on they’ve been adjusted with the Color page’s HDR toolset. 
	 Magic Mask: Filters photos based on if they’ve used the Color page’s Magic Mask tool.
	 Noise Reduction: Filters photos based on if they’ve used the Color page’s 
Noise Reduction toolset.

	 Open FX: Filters photos based on if they have an effect applied.

Adding Versions in a Photo Album
One useful feature of a Photo Album is its versioning feature. You can make adjustments to your photo, 
save it as a version, then try something radically different on the same image, knowing that the original 
version is safely stored. You can save an unlimited number of versions of an image.
It’s easy to create a version, make your edits, then right-click on a photo in the Photo Album and select 
New Version from the context menu. This will open up the New Version dialog box, where you can add 
a descriptive name for your version and then click on the OK button.
The New Version dialog box	
The Version Dropdown at the  
bottom of the Photo Viewer
It’s equally easy to switch versions too. Any saved versions are in the exact same right-click context 
menu you created it with. In addition, there’s a simple dropdown selector at the bottom of the Photo 
Viewer you can use.
IMPORTANT: Only the currently selected version will be exported in Quick Export and the 
Deliver page. All other versions will be ignored.
Integrating Photo Albums with 
Other Pages in DaVinci Resolve
Photo Albums are also used to move still photos at their native resolution between the different pages 
in DaVinci Resolve. Effectively, Photo Albums translate the single-frame nature of photos into a format 
that can be understood by the other pages. This means that in addition to the Photo page, you can use 
the tools in the Color page and Fusion page on your still photos too.
592
Photo | Chapter 28 Using Photo Albums
PHOTO

===== Page 593 =====
NOTE: When moving into a different page, each still photo will have a default time duration 
assigned to it. When returning to the Photo page, this duration will collapse again. If you wish 
to change the default time duration of a still photo, go to DaVinci Resolve > Preferences > 
User > Editing > General Settings, and set a new value in the Standard still duration field.
Using Photo Albums with the Color Page
To take advantage of DaVinci Resolve’s extensive motion picture color grading toolset, consider 
bringing your Photo Album into the Color page for photo editing. You can now apply the same color 
grading tools used in major films to edit your photos. The Photo Album transforms into a standard 
timeline while you’re using the Color page’s grading tools. When you’re finished, the results are 
reflected in your album on in the Photo page. If you have a DaVinci Resolve control surface, such as a 
Micro or Mini Color panel, you can use all the controls to edit your photos with tactile precision. 
NOTE: The edits you make in the Photo page automatically become the image’s first Node 
when you bring it into the Color page.
A Photo Album in the Color page.
In this case, we brought a Photo Album into Color, and used the Color Warper tool to alter the woman’s 
hair color to a darker shade of green, while leaving the rest of the image unchanged.

Photo | Chapter 28 Using Photo Albums
PHOTO

===== Page 594 =====
Using Photo Albums with the Fusion Page
Bringing a Photo Album into the Fusion page turns the application from a photo editor into a photo 
compositor. Fusion’s deep compositing toolset lets you creatively use masks, keying, text, and a real 
3D space to modify and enhance your still images.
A Photo Album in the Fusion page.
In this instance, we brought a Photo Album into Fusion, and set up a node tree that first created the 
titles using the Multitext tool—then took that composited image into a 3D space to scale and rotate it.
We then brought the image back into the Photo page for export in its original resolution, and as a high 
dpi image suitable for printing.
Using Photo Albums with 
Cut, Edit, and Fairlight Pages
Due to the non-temporal nature of the Photo Album, there’s not much that you can do with it in the 
Cut, Edit, or Fairlight pages, other than view the album as a timeline. These pages are designed to 
work with moving video and audio clips. However, you can export an album’s final image from the 
Photo page, and then re-import it as a normal still for use in video projects.

Image Editing in the Photo Page
Image editing in the Photo page is non-destructive, since your edits are stored in your Photo 
Album. This means your original photos are never altered, and your changes are saved in your 
DaVinci Resolve Project. 
Most image editing tools are in the Inspector, but you can also find some visual-oriented adjustments 
in the Tools interface (bottom left of the Viewer).
NOTE: All grades and effects for still images within albums are applied at the source level. 
If you add the same image to multiple Photo Albums in the same project, changing that image 
in one album will also change it in the other one. You can get around this issue by using 
image Versions.
The Viewer
The Photo Viewer is the largest viewer in DaVinci Resolve, and gives you a detailed look at high-
resolution images while you’re editing them. It also has its own toolset to work with your photos.
The Photo Viewer

Bypass Color and Fusion: To bypass any Color or Fusion effects that have been

Custom Guides and Snapping in the Viewer
When you create custom guides in the viewer, you can fully customize and create specific geographic 
locations in the frame—then have the image snap to those locations in other operations. You can 
create Guides, which are colored lines that cross the frame horizontally or vertically, and Rulers, which 
provide measurement metrics along the edges of the frame. Both Guides and Rulers are overlay tools 
for adjusting your video position, and only show in the Viewer, not your final project output.
The Viewer with Guides and Rulers enabled
To show Guides and Rulers independently, go to the Viewer Guides dropdown menu on the 
Viewer, then click on their corresponding icons in the Ruler Guides section.

the Viewer.
Pixel: Shows the ruler in number of pixels from the origin point (0,0) in the middle of the frame using 
a standard x/y cartesian coordinate graph, that reflects the Position field in the Video Inspector.
Percentage: Shows the ruler in percentage distance from the origin point (0%, 0%) in the top-left of 
the frame. The top ruler runs from 0% at the left to 100% at the right, while the side ruler measures 
0% from the top to 100% at the bottom. For example, a point at the exact center of the frame would 
be at (50%, 50%).
The Add/Edit Guide dialog
To Show and Create a Guide Line:
1	
Activate the Guides by choosing View > Guides > On. Alternatively, go to the Viewer Guides 
dropdown in the Timeline Viewer and click on the Guides icon.
2	
Create a new Guide by choosing View > Guides > Add Guide. Alternatively, right-click on the Ruler 
in the Viewer and select Add Guides.
3	
In the Add Guides dialog, choose the position and orientation of your new guide, and click Add.
Units: Choose which metric you want the guideline to use. Pixel shows the number of pixels from 
the guide’s origin point, while Percentage shows the percentage distance from the top left of the 
frame at 0%,0%.
Position: Enter a value for where in the frame you want the guideline to intersect. You can 
also click and drag this line in the viewer to position it by eye (a small pop-up will reveal the 
exact position value as you move it). To prevent this guide from being moved accidentally, 
click the lock icon.
Orientation: Choose either a horizontal or vertical orientation for the line.
Color: Choose the color of the guideline from the available options.
To Modify a Guideline:
	 Click and drag the line to any position in the viewer. A small pop-up window will indicate the exact 
position value.
	 To change the color of the Guidelines for legibility, right-click in the Ruler and select a new color 
from the Guide Color context menu.
	 To delete a line, right-click that line in the viewer and choose Remove Guide.
	 To change an existing line’s position and orientation, right-click on it in the Viewer and choose 
Edit Guide.
	 To delete all lines, only horizontal lines, or only vertical lines, choose View > Guides and choose 
which lines you want removed. Alternatively, simply right-click on the Ruler.

Photo Preview Resolution
Because Photo uses the native resolution of your media, processing times depend on your camera’s 
photo formats. Larger formats could slow down your workstation significantly.
To keep performance snappy, the Photo page uses a reduced preview resolution in the Viewer. 
You can adjust the parameters of this setting via Playback > Photo Album Preview Resolution.
The options are:
	 Auto (default): Downscales any photo over 4K in resolution to 4K size for preview.
	 Full: Photo will use the full-sized resolution of the image preview, regardless of 
performance issues.
	 Half: Reduces the photo resolution by half the size for image preview.
	 Quarter: Reduces the photo resolution to one quarter the size for image preview.
NOTE: This setting is used for previewing the working image only. On export, 
DaVinci Resolve will always use the original full-sized image for final output.
Bypass Color Grades and Fusion
To improve playback performance on low power computers, use the Bypass Color Grades and Fusion 
Effects button/dropdown to disable all applied grading and effects. Click the button (Shift-D) to disable 
or re-enable grading and effects, or right-click the same button to access a menu that lets you choose 
which page you want this button to bypass.
Right-click the Bypass Grades and Fusion button to view the available options

RAW
These tools let you edit the image using its pre-debayered RAW data settings. RAW editing uses 
pure sensor data and is generally tuned to your specific camera, so it is the preferred way to adjust 
exposure and color. If your file is not  in a RAW format, this tab will be grayed out. Each RAW parameter 
can be reset individually by clicking on the reset icon to the right of the control.
Your file’s RAW settings may vary based on the camera manufacturer, so it’s best to refer to your 
camera’s documentation manual. Below are the common controls for RAW de-bayering:
	 Decode Quality: Lets you de-bayer RAW files at Full, Half, or Quarter resolution to improve 
performance on slower systems. Lower resolution media has a quicker processing time. If you’re 
working on a low-power system, choose a lower resolution setting for better real-time playback—
then switch to a higher quality when rendering the final output. To adjust the decode quality for all 
photos based on the project settings, select Project Settings.
	 White Balance: The first option uses the white balance that was as shot in camera. The other 
options offer White Balance presets, which automatically adjust the Temperature and Tint 
parameters. These options include Daylight, Cloudy, Shade, Tungsten, Fluorescent, and Flash.
	 Color Space: Choose your preferred color space for editing and delivering the photo. In RAW 
settings, it’s generally advised to use a color space from your camera’s manufacturer, or choose a 
color space for common video standards.
	 Gamma: Choose the gamma curve to apply to the image. Either one from your camera’s 
manufacturer, or specific gammas for common video standards.
	 Color Temp: Adjusts the white balance color temperature to alter the “warmth” of the image. 
Adjustable in degrees Kelvin. Lower values correct for “warmer” lighting, while higher values 
correct for “cool” lighting.
607
Photo | Chapter 29 Editing Images in the Photo Page
PHOTO

===== Page 608 =====
	 Tint: Alters the green to magenta balance of the image (for images with fluorescent tinting). Lower 
values add green to balance out magenta lighting, while higher values add magenta to balance 
out green lighting.
	 Exposure: Increases or lowers image lightness in units relative to ƒ-stops. If your intended 
exposure adjustment lifts image data above the maximum white level, don’t worry; all image data 
is preserved and can be retrieved in subsequent adjustments. 0 is unity. The range is –5 to +5.
	 Sharpness: A debayer-specific sharpness filter applied to provide the appearance of enhanced 
image detail. 10 is unity. The range is 0 to 100.
	 Noise Reduction: This slider adjusts noise reduction on the image. Typically, high ISO images or 
darker photos will require some noise reduction.
	 Highlights: Lets you selectively retrieve blown-out highlight detail in high-dynamic-range media 
by lowering this parameter, and achieves a smooth blend between the retrieved highlights and the 
unadjusted midtones for a natural result. 0 is unity. The range is -100 to +100.
	 Shadows: Lets you selectively lighten or darken shadow detail. Raising this value retrieves 
shadow detail recorded below 0 percent, while leaving the midtones as is. 0 is unity. The range is 
-100 to +100.
	 Color Boost: Lets you increase or lower the saturation of regions of low saturation, sometimes 
referred to as a vibrance operation. 0 is unity. The range is -100 to +100.
	 Saturation: Adjusts the color intensity of the image. 0 is unity. The range is -100 to +100.
	 Lift: Adjusts the black point of the media, raising or lowering it while scaling all midtone values 
between it and the white point. Regardless of your adjustments, all image data is preserved and 
can be retrieved in subsequent adjustments. The range is -100 to +100.
	 Midtone Detail: When this parameter is raised, the contrast of regions of the image with high edge 
detail is raised to increase the perception of image sharpness, sometimes referred to as definition. 
When this parameter is lowered to a negative value, regions of the image with low amounts of 
detail are softened, while areas of high detail are left alone. 0 is unity. The range is -100 to +100.
	 Gain: Adjusts the white point of the media, raising or lowering it while scaling all midtone values 
between it and the black point. Regardless of your adjustments, all image data is preserved and 
can be retrieved in subsequent adjustments. 0 is unity. The range is -100 to +100.
	 Contrast: Raising contrast reduces shadows and raises highlights, while leaving midtones at 
50 percent unaffected. Regardless of your adjustments, all image data is preserved and can be 
retrieved in subsequent adjustments. 0 is unity. The range is -100 to +100.

Source Transform
	 Zoom X/Y: Enlarges or shrinks an image. The X and Y parameters can be linked to lock the aspect 
ratio of the image, or released to stretch or squeeze the image in one direction only.
	 Position X/Y: Moves the image within the frame, allowing pan and scan adjustments to be made. 
X moves the image left or right, and Y moves the image up or down.
	 Rotation Angle: Rotates the image around the center point.
	 Pitch: Rotates the image toward or away from the camera along an axis running through the 
center of the image, from left to right. Positive values push the top of the image away and bring 
the bottom of the image forward. Negative values bring the top of the image forward and push the 
bottom of the image away. Higher values will stretch the image to larger extremes.
	 Yaw: Rotates the image toward or away from the camera along an axis running through the center 
of the image from top to bottom. Positive values bring the left of the image forward and push the 
right of the image away. Negative values push the left of the image away and pull the right of the 
image forward. Higher values will stretch the image to larger extremes.
	 Flip Image: Two buttons let you flip the image in different dimensions.
Flip Horizontal control: Reverses the image along the X axis, left to right.
Flip Vertical control: Reverses the clip along the Y axis, turning it upside down.
Source Cropping
	 Ratio: Choose a width-to-height ratio for the image. You can choose from common still photo 
ratios, or leave it As Shot to use your camera’s native ratio.
	 Lock Aspect Ratio: Check this box to lock the aspect ratio when using cropping functions. Once 
locked, the photo’s original aspect ratios remain even while cropping. When unlocked, the photo’s 
aspect ratio changes during cropping.
	 Crop Left/Right/Top/Bottom: Lets you cut off, in pixels, the four sides of the image.
Looks
	 Type: Apply a preset Look filter from the dropdown menu, or leave it as Default (Original) to 
bypass the Look filters.
Adjustments
	 Auto Balance: A one-button solution that automatically adjusts the dynamic range and white 
balance based on machine learning.
	 Temp: Lets you adjust the image along a warm/orange to cool/blue axis that corresponds to the 
naturalistic spectrum of color temperatures used for lighting. Raise this parameter to adjust the 
color balance towards warm/orange tones, or lower the parameter to a negative value to adjust 
the color balance towards blue/cyan tones.
	 Tint: Lets you adjust the image along a magenta to green axis that corresponds to the color 
temperatures found in artificial lighting sources, such as fluorescent and sodium vapor lighting 
fixtures. Raise this parameter to adjust the color balance towards magenta tones (sometimes 
referred to as “minus green” to correct for fluorescent lighting), or lower the parameter to a 
negative value to adjust the color balance towards green tones (“plus green” to correct for other 
kinds of lighting).
	 Lift: Lets you adjust the perceived shadow density of the image by altering the black point of the 
image. Drag the Lift slider to the left to darken the darkest values in the image, which increases 
the distance between the black and white points of the image and stretches the midtone values 
in-between. Drag the Lift slider to the right to lighten the darkest values in the image, which 
reduces contrast and squeezes all the midtone values between the black and white points.
609
Photo | Chapter 29 Editing Images in the Photo Page
PHOTO

===== Page 610 =====
	 Gamma: Lets you adjust the overall perceived lightness of the image. It works by altering the 
distribution of midtones that fall between the Lift and Gain master wheel settings. Dragging 
the Gamma master wheel to the left darkens the overall image, while dragging it to the right 
brightens it. 
	 Gain: Lets you adjust the lightness of the highlights by altering the white point of the image. 
Dragging the Gain slider to the left makes the lightest values of the image darker, squeezing the 
midtones between the white and black points of the image. Dragging Gain to the right makes the 
lightest values even lighter, eventually clipping at maximum white.
	 Contrast: The Contrast parameters let you quickly narrow or widen image contrast about a user-
definable pivot point. This one parameter lets you increase or reduce the distance between the 
darkest and lightest values of an image, raising or lowering image contrast. 
	 Pivot: Changes the center of tonality, so that dark and bright parts of the image are stretched or 
narrowed during a contrast adjustment. Darker images may require a lower Pivot value to avoid 
“crushing” the shadows when stretching image contrast. Lighter images may benefit from a higher 
Pivot value to increase shadow density adequately.
	 Midtone Details: Raising this parameter increases the contrast of high-detail edges, enhancing the 
perceived image sharpness of the image (this is also known as definition). Lowering this parameter 
to a negative value softens areas with less detail while leaving high-detail regions as is.
	 Shadows: Lets you selectively lighten or darken shadow detail. Raising this value retrieves shadow 
detail recorded below 0 percent, while leaving the midtones alone.
	 Highlights: Lower this parameter to selectively retrieve blown-out highlight detail in high-
dynamic-range media—this results in a smooth blend between the retrieved highlights and the 
unadjusted midtones.
	 Saturation: A uniform saturation operation that raises (above 50) or lowers (below 50) the color 
intensity of every color value within the image. 50 is unity, showing unaltered saturation. The 
range is 0 (completely desaturated) through +100 (saturation is doubled).
	 Hue: Rotates all hues of the image around the full perimeter of the color wheel. The default setting 
of 50 shows the original distribution of hues. Raising or lowering this value rotates all hues forward 
or backward along the hue distribution as seen on a color wheel.

Adding and Exporting LUTs
If you’ve installed a custom or pre-made Look Up Table (LUT) into DaVinci Resolve, any photo in the 
Media Pool or the Photo Album can have a LUT applied to it. To do so simply right-click the photo’s 
thumbnail and choose the LUT from the LUT context menu.
To save a look for use in other projects and photos, create your own LUT by right-clicking on the image 
in the Photo Album, and selecting Generate LUT from the context menu. Generally the 33 Point Cube 
option is the most compatible. You will then need to re-import that LUT back into DaVinci Resolve.
NOTE: Generally only settings in the Photo tab carry over into the LUT. RAW adjustments and 
Effects will not be saved into the LUT.
For more information on using LUTs, jump to this chapter: Using LUTs.

Copy and Paste Edits Between Images
To apply the same edit from one image to another photo (or photos) in your album, either: directly 
apply the effect in the Photo Album, or use the copy and paste attributes function.
Applying Edits From One Photo to Another in an Album
To copy-paste an edit from one image to another in the same Photo Album:
1	
Select the photo(s) you want to apply the edits on. These photos will be highlighted.
2	
Middle-mouse click on the photo whose edits you want to copy.
3	
The effect will be copied to the your selected photos.
NOTE: This operation will not copy any applied effects. It will copy RAW settings, as long as 
the images involved all are the same RAW format file type.
Copy and Paste Photo Attributes
You can copy-paste photo attributes and effects from one clip to multiple clips with the Paste 
Attributes command.
To copy attributes:
1	
Select a photo whose attributes you want to apply to other clips, and press Command-C.
2	
Select one or more other photos to paste to.
3	
Choose Edit > Paste Attributes (Option-V), or right-click one of the selected clips and choose Paste 
Attributes from the contextual menu.
4	
When the Paste Attributes window appears, enable the checkboxes of your chosen attributes, 
then click Apply.

Using DaVinci Resolve Color Panels 
with Photo
Many of the attributes and parameters in the Photo page are functionally mapped to Blackmagic’s 
DaVinci Resolve Color Panel hardware options, including the Micro Color, Mini, and Advanced panels. 
This lets you edit photos with the tactile and precision handling of a dedicated hardware interface. 
For detailed information on how your specific Color Panel maps to the Photo page, refer to your 
panel’s documentation.
Photo Multiuser Collaboration and 
Blackmagic Cloud Syncing
The Photo page lets you take advantage of DaVinci Resolve’s extensive Multiuser collaboration 
and Blackmagic Cloud tools. For example, using Capture Live View in a collaboration project, lets 
another user view the video feed online from another location. You can also sync and store photos in 
a Blackmagic Cloud Folder, allowing multiple users around the world access to your photo edits, as 
week as make changes collaboratively.
For more information on using these tools, see the Blackmagic Cloud section of this manual.
Photo Editing Example
Having a still image editor embedded in DaVinci Resolve’s film and video editing tools opens you up 
to a spectrum of creative and practical photo effects.
As an example, let’s edit this image (taken on a standard phone camera) to look like it was shot on 
35mm motion picture film.
First, use the Photo Inspector to adjust the image’s exposure and color balance.
The original image, taken on a standard camera phone
614
Photo | Chapter 29 Editing Images in the Photo Page
PHOTO

===== Page 615 =====
In this image, the details on the statues (in the foreground) seem to blend into the background. 
This is because the entire image is in sharp focus.
To fix this, drag DaVinci Resolve’s new CineFocus effect on top of the image in the album to create 
a virtual lens with a larger aperture, shallower depth of field characteristics, and improved bokeh.
CineFocus first analyzes the photo to create a Depth Map of perceived distances inside 
the 2D image.
The CineFocus Depth Map analyzes which parts of the image are  
in the foreground (brighter) and which are in the background (darker)
Then using Focus mode, adjust the aperture and depth of field to isolate the foreground statues, 
while pushing everything in the background out of focus.
The CineFocus Focus mode lets you set a new focus distance  
and depth of field (color images) vs out of focus areas (white)
615
Photo | Chapter 29 Editing Images in the Photo Page
PHOTO

===== Page 616 =====
Now tweak the exact lens parameters to your liking. In this example, we’ve gone from a basic 
virtual lens to an 11-bladed anamorphic lens with some chromatic aberration, and a slightly off-
center lens curvature.
In this CineFocus image, the background is now blurred. The blur also increases gradually 
with distance, which is more realistic than simply masking an area and blurring it
The image now looks like it was shot on a cinematic lens. To complete the effect so that it appears 
to have been shot on 35mm motion picture film, drag the Film Look Creator effect on top of the 
image in the Photo Album. We now have two effects working on the same image simultaneously.
The Film Look Creator lets you adjust film parameters like halation, grain, bloom, vignetting etc. 
In this case, we’ve gone with the Default 35mm film preset, which adds a filmic color profile with 
the a convincing grain pattern.
The finished image, with the Film Look Creator applied
The statues now appear more striking against the background, and the entire frame has been 
treated with a filmic look.

The Effects Library
The Effects panel contains a hierarchical, categorized list of all of the effects and filters you can add to 
your photos:
The Photo Effects library
Previewing an Effect
To preview an effect before placing it on a photo, ensure that Hover Scrub Preview is checked in 
the Effects option menu—it should be, by default. Then hover your pointer over any thumbnail in 
the Effects tab and move it across the thumbnail. The effect will preview on the image in the Viewer 
using its default parameters.
619
Photo | Chapter 30 Photo Effects
PHOTO

===== Page 620 =====
Hover the pointer over an effect (orange rectangle) to preview that effect on the image in the viewer
Searching the Effects Library
Use the search bar at the top of the Effects Library to search for a particular effect. Pressing shift-
space will bring up the Effects Search dialog in the Photo page. If you have a photo selected, 
double‑click on the effect in the search list to apply that effect to the selected photo.
You can search for effects and transitions using Category Names as a search term. 
For example, searching for Stylize will bring up all the Resolve FX under the Stylize section. You can 
also search for effects using the language set in DaVinci Resolve > Preferences > User > UI Settings, 
in addition to English.
Applying an Effect
You can apply an effect on a single image, or bulk-apply that effect on multiple images in an album. 
You can do so in the following ways:
To apply an effect to a photo in an album:
1	
Drag the thumbnail of the selected effect to any photo in the Album
2	
OR double-click on an effect in the Effects Library to apply it to the selected photo in the album.
To apply an effect to multiple photos in an album:
1	
Select the photos you want to apply the effect to in the album, either by command-clicking 
(multiple selection), or shift-clicking (range). To select all the photos in an album, use command-A.
2	
Double-click on the effect in the Effects Library you want to apply.
NOTE: You can apply as many effects to a photo as you want. They will stack up in the 
Inspector under the Effects tab.

Favoriting Effects
If you have an effect that you use often, you can right-click on the effect’s thumbnail and select Add to 
Favorites from the context menu. Alternatively, you can click on the small star icon in its thumbnail to 
favorite it. 
Favorited effects show up in the Favorites tab in the Effects Library. This gives you quick access to 
your most-used effects.
To remove an effect from Favorites, right-click on its thumbnail and select Remove from Favorites in 
the context menu. Alternatively, you can simply click the star icon again.
NOTE: Favoriting an effect does not save any custom attributes you may have previously set. 
The effect will subsequently apply with its default values.
Editing an Effect
When you select a photo with an effect on it, you can edit and adjust the effect’s parameters by 
opening Inspector and choosing the Effects tab. This will show you every parameter associated with 
that effect, ready for customization. 
If more than one effect is applied to a photo, they will all be stacked in the Effects tab, and will work on 
the image sequentially from top to bottom. You can rearrange the order of an effect by clicking on the 
up and down arrows next to the effect’s name in the Effects tab.
Adjust any of the standard controls to manipulate that plugin’s effect on the image, which will be 
reflected in the viewer.
The parameters of the Film Damage effect, 
located in the Inspector > Effects tab.

Resolve FX Onscreen Controls
In addition to the parameters in Inspector, some effects also use onscreen controls that can be 
manipulated in the viewer. Different effects expose different custom controls, letting you control the 
effect or manipulate the image, depending on that effect’s function.
The Lens Flare effect has an onscreen control which lets you adjust the 
size of the flare in the viewer by dragging the mouse.
When an effect has an onscreen control, you will need to enable Effects Overlay mode in the viewer 
to see it. Generally, the effect will open and set this mode by default. However, you can also set it 
yourself by clicking on the Tools icon at the bottom of the viewer, then clicking on the Effects Overlay 
icon, and selecting either Open FX Overlay (if using a Resolve FX), or Fusion Overlay (if using a 
Fusion Effect).
To display onscreen controls for an effect, click on the Tools icon (circled red) then 
select the Effects Overlay icon (red underline), and choose an overlay type.
TIP: You can temporarily hide or show the onscreen controls in the Viewer, which gives you 
a cleaner interface when adjusting your image. These onscreen controls can be toggled off 
and on by pressing shift-` (tilde).

Removing or Disabling an Effect
If you’ve changed your mind about an effect, you can either remove it entirely, or disable its output 
(while still retaining the custom parameters you set up) in Inspector.
To remove an existing effect on a photo:
1	
Open Inspector.
2	
Click on the Effects tab.
3	
Find the effect you wish to remove.
4	
Click on the small trash-can icon to the right of its name.
To disable an existing effect on a photo:
1	
Open Inspector.
2	
Click on the Effects tab.
3	
Find the effect you wish to remove.
4	
Click on the orange toggle switch next to its name. To enable the effect again, toggle the switch 
once more.
Copy and Pasting an Effect
To copy and paste an effect (with its custom parameters) from one photo to another, use the Paste 
Attributes window. Here’s how:
To copy an effect from one photo to another:
1	
In your chosen album, select the photo that you want to copy the effect from.
2	
Right-click on the photo and choose Copy Attributes (command-C) from the context menu.
3	
Go to the photo you want to paste the effect to, then right-click and choose Paste Attributes 
(Option-V) from the context menu.
4	
In the Paste Attributes window that appears, check the box next to Plugins in the Photo 
Attributes settings.
5	
Uncheck any checkboxes from other attributes that you do not want to copy from the 
original photo.
6	
Click Apply.
The effect will then be pasted into the Effects tab of the new photo, which you can use as-is or 
continue to manipulate.
For more information on using the Paste Attributes window, jump to this chapter:  
Editing Images in the Photo Page.

Capture (Studio Version Only)
This tab opens up the Capture Live View interface for tethered shooting directly from your camera 
into DaVinci Resolve. This lets you instantly transfer your shots to the Media Pool or a Photo Album for 
editing, client review, or just to see your image in higher resolution on a larger screen. 
Setting up Camera Tethering
To start, set up Camera Tethering on your camera. This is dependent on your camera model and its 
make, so it’s best to refer to your camera manual for specifics.
Next, connect your camera to your DaVinci Resolve Workstation with a USB cable. Your local 
computer may require some additional setup.
Supported Cameras for Camera Tethering
The following cameras are supported for live preview, control, and capture in the Photo page:
	 Canon EOS: Most modern models.
	 Fujifilm: GFX 100, GFX 50R, GFX 50S, GFX ETERNA 55, GFX100 II, GFX100RF, GFX100S, 
GFX100S II, GFX50S II, X-H2, X-H2S, X-M5, X-Pro3, X-S10, X-S20, X-T3, X-T4 and X-T5.
	 Leica: SL-2, SL-3.
	 Sony: Most modern models, including the a7R VI.
Windows users require additional Sony software to be installed for tethering support.
macOS supports Sony cameras natively.

and Tethering.

Camera Tethering Troubleshooting Tips:
If you’re having trouble connecting your camera to DaVinci Resolve, try these troubleshooting tips:
	 Ensure you have no other open programs that automatically connect to the camera, such as photo 
editing applications.
	 Sometimes, you may need to restart DaVinci Resolve to connect to your camera.
Once your camera and computer system are set up, press the Capture tab to automatically 
connect to your camera. You can also press the Capture Live View icon at the top of the viewer to 
go to the Capture Live View interface.
In the right-hand column, you’ll see capture controls based on your camera model. You’ll also 
be able to change your camera settings from the capture interface. 
In addition, the top toolbar lets you adjust settings for aperture, shutter speed, ISO and 
exposure compensation. Directly underneath it, you can adjust focus by rotating the wheel 
or pressing the direction buttons. For extra granularity, go further down in Settings to access 
more advanced camera settings. Unsupported camera settings will be grayed out. 
To the immediate left is Capture Live View, which updates in real-time based on what your 
camera sees—including on-screen displays such as focus boxes and focus peaking.
The display to the far left is the most recent photo that you captured, so you can see the 
difference between it and your current shot setup. You can pause Live View at any time by 
toggling the Capture Live View slider.
Once you’re happy with the live view in your camera, go ahead and capture the image by 
pressing the shutter release button in the upper right of the capture controls.
Capture
This toolset lets you control your camera and capture images.
	 Camera Name: The model of camera that is connected to capture.
	 Half Press: Click this icon to send a half-press signal to the camera, often used to lock autofocus 
before firing the shutter.
	 Shutter Release: Click this icon to activate the camera’s shutter release and take a photo.
	 Aperture: Shows the currently selected aperture of the camera lens.
	 Shutter Speed: Shows the currently selected Shutter Speed of the camera.
	 ISO: Shows the currently selected ISO of the camera.
	 Exposure Compensation: Shows the currently selected exposure compensation of the camera.
	 AutoFocus: Click this icon to set the autofocus.
	 Control Wheel: Depending on which parameter is active and controllable, you can use the control 
wheel and the arrow controls to adjust that parameter.
	 Enable Capture Live Preview: Activate this toggle switch to turn on Live Camera Preview in 
the viewer.

Scopes
The scopes here are identical to those found in Inspector. The selected scope will update in real-time 
from the camera data.
Settings
These settings let you directly control the tethered camera from the Capture interface. Depending on 
your camera model and its make, some or all of these modes may be disabled.
	 Shooting Mode: Sets a shooting mode for the camera. Common modes are A (aperture priority), S 
(shutter priority), P (program), and M (manual). The options available to you depend on your camera 
model and its make.
	 Aperture: Sets the lens’ aperture.
	 Shutter: Sets the camera’s shutter speed.
	 ISO: Sets the camera’s ISO.
	 Exposure Comp: Sets the number of stops of for the camera’s exposure compensation.
	 White Balance: Sets the camera’s white balance setting preset.
	 Temperature: Sets an exact white balance temperature in degrees Kelvin (K).
	 Drive: Sets the camera’s drive mode. Common modes are Timer, High Frame Rate, and so on. 
The choices available to you are dependent on your camera model and its make.
	 Focus Mode: Sets the camera’s focus mode. Common modes are AF-S, AF-C, Manual, and so 
on—but these depend on your camera model and its make.
	 Focus Area: Sets the camera’s focus area for automatic focus settings. Common modes are Wide, 
Center, Zone, and so on—but these depend on your camera model and its make.
	 File Settings: Sets the format you want the image captured in. Common formats are RAW, .jpg, 
RAW+.jpg, and so on. The choices available to you depend on your camera model and its make.
	 File Size: Sets the file size of the photo format.
Production
This toolset is designed to help with file and photo management operations.
	 File Name: Lets you set up automatic file name conventions using combinations of text 
and metadata variables (activated by first typing in the % symbol) for your subsequently 
captured photos.
	 Custom Name: Type in a more human-readable photo name that will reflect in the Media Pool 
without interfering with the original file name.
	 Production Name: Lets you type in a production (shoot) name to add this field for 
organizational purposes.
	 Location: Click the browse button to open a file requester to choose where to store the 
captured photos.
	 Add To Bin: Lets you select a Media Pool bin for the captured photos to be automatically added to.
	 Add to Album: Select an album for the captured photos to be automatically added to.
	 Keywords: Add specific keywords to describe the photo for organizational purposes.
	 Auto Select Latest Captured Image: Check this box to always select the last-captured image in 
the interface for further modification.

Quick Export opens a simple delivery window that’s designed specifically for still images. 
Simply select the image format you want to use on the left side, enter the file’s parameters 
on the right—you can also view the selected photo’s file information here—then click Export. 
Quick Export tab in the Photo Page

file sizes.

	 Resolution: Sets the resolution of the photo in ppi (pixels per inch). 72 is the standard for video

	 Export: Choose Entire Album to export all photos in the album, or Selected Photos to export only 
the photos you’ve selected in the album at the bottom of the Deliver page.

Chapter 33
Using the Cut Page
The Cut page is a focused environment for fast editing. It’s useful in situations where you need 
to quickly cut a news segment, build an episode of web content, edit a straightforward program, 
experiment with multiple arrangements of a scene, or put together a first assembly edit. 
The Cut page is also a good introductory editing interface for people who are new to editing, as it 
presents a streamlined set of tools that are fast to learn and simple to use. Whatever your background, 
you’ll find the Cut page to be a valuable addition to your editing experience in DaVinci Resolve.

Overview of the Cut Page
With the addition of the Cut page, DaVinci Resolve now has two editing environments, intended for 
two different audiences. While the Cut and Edit pages share many of the same panels such as the 
Media Pool, the Timeline, and the Viewer, the controls that are exposed on the Cut page have been 
designed for speed, so you can cut professional programs faster than you’ve ever been able to before.
Overview of the Cut Page User Interface
The default workspace of the Cut page consists of the Media Pool, a single Viewer, and the 
Timeline area. These three regions let you quickly import and organize clips, edit clips, and even 
export the result, all from within the Cut page.
The Cut page interface
Customizing the UI
A User Interface toolbar at the top of the Cut page lets you hide and show different panels as 
necessary. For example, you can hide the Media Pool if you wanted more room for the Viewer. 
You can also replace the Media Pool with other browsers in the Media Pool’s default area, showing 
the Sync Bin, Transitions, Titles, or Effects Browser in order to add those effects to your program in 
the Timeline. On the right side of the User Interface toolbar you can perform a Quick Export, expand 
the Viewer to Full Screen, or open the Inspector.
Separate tabs on the left let you open the Media Pool,  
Sync Bin, Keyframe Editor, Transitions, Titles, and Effects browser.

The Media Pool
The Media Pool contains all video clips, audio clips, graphics, and other media that you import into 
your project. You can create bins with which to organize all of this media, to make it easier to find what 
you need quickly. These bins are opened via the bin dropdown at the upper left-hand corner.
Each piece of media you import, whether it’s video, audio, or graphics, appears as an individual clip 
and can be selected, scrubbed for fast viewing, reorganized into bins, opened into the Viewer for 
playback, or edited into a timeline using the edit buttons or via drag and drop.
The Media Pool in Thumbnail view
View icons at the upper right of the Media Pool let you see your clips in different ways, depending on 
what you need to accomplish.
The Viewing ModeFs buttons
Metadata view: Each clip is represented by its own card with a scrubbable thumbnail 
and basic clip metadata information visible. This view is designed to have more 
metadata information than a thumbnail view but more targeted information than the 
List view. 
Thumbnail view: Each clip is represented by a scrubbable thumbnail. Hover the 
playhead over each thumbnail and move it left and right to see the clip’s image play, 
and use the I and O keys to mark sections of a clip that you want to use. Clicking on the 
lower right corner of a thumbnail reveals the clip’s metadata.
Filmstrip view: Each clip is represented by a filmstrip of consecutive frames the length 
of the Media Pool. Hover the playhead over the clip and move it left and right to see 
the clip’s image play, and use the I and O keys to mark sections of a clip that you 
want to use.
List view: Each clip appears as an item in a multi-column list showing a variety of 
metadata about each clip. In List view, you can click the header of any column to sort 
the contents by that column’s information (clicking again toggles the sort order between 
Ascending and Descending). Scrolling right reveals additional columns of information.

Optimized UI Layouts for Vertical Editing
Optimized layouts for vertical timelines and projects are supported in DaVinci Resolve. When a vertical 
timeline or project is loaded, the UI automatically switches to a layout optimized for vertical viewers 
on the Cut, Edit, and Color pages. Loading a normal landscape timeline or project then automatically 
switches back to the original layout. No additional user intervention is needed. 
You can change this behavior in Preferences > User > UI Settings > Use optimized UI layouts 
for vertical video. Unchecking this box retains the normal horizontal layout, even for vertical 
video timelines.
The UI now changes format to accommodate vertical video timelines automatically.
